YYYPlain language summary: Does surgery for stroke due to bleeding in the brain improve the chance of people being able to function and live independently or cause any unwanted effects?

Key messages

• In adults with stroke due to bleeding in the brain, surgical removal of the bleeding may increase the chance of people being able to function independently and may reduce the risk of dying compared to people who are treated with standard medical care alone. We are very uncertain if surgical removal of the bleeding has an effect on quality of life after a stroke due to bleeding in the brain.

• It is uncertain if partial removal of the skull without removal of the bleeding has an effect on the ability to function independently, death, and quality of life after a brain haemorrhage, as there was only one study.

• More high-quality trials with more people with stroke due to bleeding in the brain are needed to find out if surgery is helpful and allow doctors to make recommendations for future clinical practice.

What is a brain haemorrhage and how is it treated?

Strokes that result from bleeding in the brain are known as brain haemorrhages. In about 20 in 100 people, the haemorrhage is caused by a problem with the structure of a blood vessel (abnormalities), trauma to the brain (for example, a blow to the head), or a brain tumour. In the remaining 80%, the haemorrhage results from damaged small blood vessels in the brain. Presently, there is no treatment that helps with brain haemorrhages, except the standard medical care provided in specialist stroke units, so-called 'bundled treatments' that rapidly correct physiological abnormalities, and possibly early control of high blood pressure. It is unknown whether surgery improves the function and lives of people with brain haemorrhages compared to standard medical care alone. Surgery for the treatment of brain haemorrhages includes:

• craniotomy (where a flap of bone is removed from the skull to access the brain) with removal of the bleeding;

• minimally invasive surgery (surgery through a small opening in the skull, with or without using a tube with a camera on it (called an endoscope), and with or without using medication to dissolve clotted blood); and

• partial removal of the skull without removal of the bleeding (which lowers the pressure in the brain and prevents further damage).

What did we want to find out?

We wanted to know if surgery improves or reduces the function and lives of people with brain haemorrhages compared to standard medical care alone. We were also interested in which surgical technique was best.

What did we do?

We searched for studies in adults with a brain haemorrhage that compared surgery plus standard medical care versus standard medical care alone. Studies could only investigate people with a brain haemorrhage that was not caused by an abnormality, trauma, or brain tumour. We compared and summarised the results of the studies and rated our confidence in the evidence, based on factors such as study methods and sizes.

What did we find?

We found 24 studies that involved 4597 people with a brain haemorrhage. Studies took place in Europe, North and South America, Asia, Africa, and Australia. The studies were published over a 35-year period from 1989 to 2024. Studies lasted for three to 12 months, with most studies lasting six months. Twenty-three studies looked at the surgical removal of brain haemorrhages, whereas one study looked at the partial removal of the skull without removal of the bleeding.

• Surgical removal of brain haemorrhages may increase the chance of being able to function independently and may reduce the risk of dying. It is unclear if surgical removal of the bleeding has an effect on quality of life after a brain haemorrhage.

• When the results were broken down by the surgical technique used to remove the bleeding, minimally invasive surgery may increase the chance of being able to function independently, but we are uncertain about this for craniotomy. However, surgical removal of the bleeding with craniotomy likely reduces the risk of death and minimally invasive surgery probably reduces the risk of death. Finally, craniotomy may make little to no difference to quality of life after a brain haemorrhage, while this is unclear for minimally invasive surgery.

• It is uncertain if partial removal of the skull without removal of the bleeding has an effect on the ability to function independently, death, and quality of life after a brain haemorrhage, as there was only one study.

What are the limitations of the evidence?

Our confidence in the evidence was moderate to very low. One important reason that lowered our confidence was how some studies were designed and conducted, which may have influenced the results. Also, some studies showed different results or only a limited number of people with a brain haemorrhage could be investigated, making the results less accurate.

How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is up to date to 11 March 2025.

YYYStudy: Juvela 1989

# YYYMethods

Study design : parallel RCT. Total study duration : four years (participant enrolment) Details of any 'run in' period: not reported. Number of study centres and location: single-centre: Helsinki University Hospital, Finland. Date of study: 1982 – 1986 (participant enrolment).

# YYYParticipants

Number randomised : 53 (surgical group: 26; conservative group: 27). Number lost to follow-up : none. Number missing (exclusions & withdrawals) : overall 1; none in the surgical group; 1 in conservative group (excluded because the ICH was found at autopsy to be due to a brain tumour not detected by CT or CTA). Number analysed : 52 (surgical group: 26; conservative group: 26). Number of cross-overs : not reported.

Baseline characteristics : mean age 51.7 years (SD 9.7) with range 24 - 65 years, male sex 58%, median GCS score 12 (IQR 7 - 14), median ICH volume 58 mL (IQR 36 - 77). ICH location: 15% lobar, 85% deep, 17% thalamic involvement, 50% left hemispheric. IVH extension 62%. The two groups were imbalanced in the GCS clinical grade, location of the haematoma and presence of IVH. The surgical group had lower GCS on admission (median 9 vs. 12) and more frequent intraventricular extension (77% vs. 46%) and thalamic involvement (31% vs. 4%). In the conservative group, a history of chronic hypertension was more frequent (77% vs. 42%).

Inclusion criteria :

* Patients with spontaneous supratentorial ICH, based on typical clinical onset, CT scans and carotid angiograms.

* Age 15 - 65 years.

* Unconscious and/or severe hemiparesis or dysphasia.

* Admitted <24 hours after the bleed.

* Possibility to receive treatment <48 hours after the bleed.

Exclusion criteria :

* Patients with cerebellar haematomas, traumatic haemorrhages, haemorrhages into brain tumours, and haemorrhages from cerebral aneurysms and AVMs.

* Patients with malignant diseases with a poor prognosis.

* Patients with severe heart, lung, or endocrine disease.

* Patients with clearly improving clinical condition.

* Patients that do not react to pain.

# YYYInterventions

Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. The operation was performed via a craniotomy immediately after randomisation. Median time from symptom onset to surgery 14.5 hours (range 6 - 48).

Standard medical management group : no description provided.

Concomitant interventions : none.

# YYYOutcomes

Death at 4 days, 1 week, 1 month, 6 months and 1 year; GOS at 1 month, 6 months and 1 year (“independent” defined as minimally or moderately disabled, which should correspond to a GOS of 4-5).

Note : GOS at 1 and 12 months was only reported as combined results for the surgical and standard medical management group and, therefore, could not be extracted.

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Random sequence generation (selection bias)** | Low risk | Details are not described in the paper, but the study author stated that treatment allocation papers were wrapped inside carbon paper and enclosed in sealed, opaque envelopes. Then the envelopes were mixed several times, like playing cards, and sequentially numbered. |
| **Allocation concealment (selection bias)** | Low risk | Details are not described in the paper, but the study author stated that sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes were used. The treatment allocation was concealed until the opening of the envelope to see how the defined patient should be treated. |
| **Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias) All outcomes** | High risk | Participants and local investigators were not blinded to treatment allocation. |
| **Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias) All outcomes** | High risk | The study author confirmed that outcome evaluations were performed by himself, who was aware of treatment allocation. Quote: "The follow-up studies were conducted by one of us (S.J.), who did not perform any of the operations." |
| **Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias) All outcomes** | Low risk | One post-randomisation exclusion because the ICH was found to be due to a brain tumour. The relevant outcome data of this participant has been provided by the study author. Therefore, the outcome data is complete. |
| **Selective reporting (reporting bias)** | High risk | The GOS was assessed 1 month, 6 months and 12 months after randomisation, but only reported for both groups separately at 6 months (at 1 and 12 months, only the combined results are reported). The original data is no longer retrievable due to administrative rules. |
| **Other bias** | Unclear risk | The two groups show a baseline imbalance in factors related to outcome after ICH: the surgical group had lower GCS on admission and more frequent intraventricular extension and thalamic involvement, which are factors associated with worse clinical outcome. |

YYYStudy: Batjer 1990

# YYYMethods

Study design : parallel RCT. Total study duration : five years and 4 months (participant enrolment). Details of any 'run in' period : not reported. Number of study centres and location : single-centre: Parkland Memorial Hospital, USA. Date of study : December 1983 – March 1989 (participant enrolment).

Notes : target sample size was 60. The trial was prematurely stopped as a result of slow patient accrual and poor functional outcome in all treatment groups. The trial has three treatment arms (best medical management, best medical management plus ICP monitoring, and surgical evacuation). For the synthesis of this review, the best medical management and best medical management plus ICP monitoring groups, were combined as the comparator intervention.

# YYYParticipants

The numbers randomised : 21 (surgical group: 8; control group: 13 (9 in the best medical management group and 4 in best medical management plus ICP monitoring group)). Number lost to follow-up : none. Number missing (exclusions & withdrawals) : none. Number analysed : 21 (surgical group: 8; control group: 13). Number of cross-overs : none (cross-over was not permitted).

Baseline characteristics : mean age 54.0 years (SD 9.9). ICH location: 100% deep (inclusion criterion) and 0% lobar. IVH extension 0%. Sex, GCS score and ICH volume are not reported. In the publication is a statement that there were no baseline imbalances between the surgical and control group in terms of age, grade on admission, SBP and DBP, or interval between onset of symptoms and arrival in the emergency department.

Inclusion criteria :

* CT evidence of classic putaminal haemorrhage ≥3.0 cm in diameter with or without ventricular extension.

* Age between 30 - 75 years.

* Documented history of hypertension (minimal prior recorded blood pressure of 160/95 mmHg).

* Patients admitted to the emergency department <24 hours of onset of symptoms.

* Patients meeting one of the three following grades: Grade 1 (alert), moderate hemiparesis (less than antigravity strength in involved arm and leg); Grade 2 (lethargic), moderate hemiparesis, severe hemiparesis (only subtle upper or lower extremity movement), or hemiplegia; and Grade 3 (obtunded, stuporous), responding only to physical stimulus, required to have at least purposeful or semi purposeful movement in their uninvolved extremities and were uniformly hemiplegic in the involved extremities.

Exclusion criteria :

* Aneurysm, AVM, or tumour (angiography required).

* Patients with decorticate or decerebrate posturing.

* Any patient with an unassociated neurologic illness, end-stage systemic disease (e.g. renal, cardiac, hepatic, or neoplastic), or coagulopathy.

# YYYInterventions

Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. Frontotemporal or pterional craniotomy with haematoma evacuation under microscopic guidance. Pharmacological blood pressure reduction by about 25% after induction of anaesthesia, with infusion of mannitol (1.0 g/kg of body weight) during the craniotomy. Thorough evacuation of clot, leaving only thin layers of coagulum adherent to particularly friable brain surfaces. In case of persistently bleeding offending lenticulostriate branches, they were selectively cauterised. After decompression was achieved, the SBP was further decreased to approximately 150 mm Hg, and from that point tightly controlled with a 150 mm Hg ceiling. Routine placement of epidural drains. Postoperative management of the patient’s airway consistent with standard postoperative care, but hyperventilation was not performed. Average time from symptom onset to surgery not reported.

Standard medical management group : a combination of two groups (for the synthesis of this review):

* Best medical management (BMM) : management in a medical ICU with the internal medicine service serving as primary physicians. Dexamethasone therapy (4 mg i.v. every 6 hours), with tapering of dosage over 7 to 14 days. Administration of appropriate antihypertensive drugs, with the goal of decreasing SBP by 25% over the first 24 hours, then slowly decreasing the target blood pressure over the next 48 - 72 hours to high-normal levels. Intermittent diuresis with furosemide and mannitol every 4 - 6 hours empirically over the first several days, with more or less frequent administration depending on the neurologic progress of the patient as well as the systemic tolerance. Intubation and mechanical hyperventilation (target pCO2 of 20 to 25 mm Hg) in all patients with decreased level of consciousness (grades 2 and 3) and in grade 1 patients who were neurologically deteriorating or who showed pulmonary compromise.

* BMM plus ICP monitoring : managed exactly as those in the BMM arm, with the exception of the placement of a frontal ventriculostomy (usually contralateral to haematoma), connected to a pressure monitor and a drainage system. The medical regimens of diuresis and hyperventilation were employed to maintain ICP levels of <20 mm Hg. When medical therapy was unsuccessful at achieving this level of control, intermittent CSF drainage was added to the treatment protocol.

Concomitant interventions : none.

# YYYOutcomes

Functional outcome assessed with own outcome scale at 3 months and 6 months (outcome Grade 3 and 4 on a 4-item scale was considered “good functional outcome” (= independent at home or returns to prestroke social activity but not necessarily to occupation)).

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Random sequence generation (selection bias)** | Low risk | Details are not described in the paper, but one of the study authors stated that the randomisation sequence was generated with a random component by herself, using either a random number table (most likely) or Cochran and Cox table of random permutations of 9. |
| **Allocation concealment (selection bias)** | Low risk | One of the study authors confirmed that sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes were used, each containing one of the three proposed treatment modalities. Quote: "Randomization was facilitated by one of us (J.S.R.) by producing a series of sealed envelopes, each containing one of the proposed treatment modalities (1, 2, or 3)." |
| **Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias) All outcomes** | High risk | Participants and local investigators were not blinded to treatment allocation. |
| **Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias) All outcomes** | High risk | Quote: “Assessments were performed by direct examination and family discussion with one of the investigators, by review of medical charts for patients being followed up in other clinic systems, or by telephone interview with family members." |
| **Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias) All outcomes** | Low risk | Outcome data of all participants are reported. |
| **Selective reporting (reporting bias)** | Low risk | All described outcomes in the methods are reported. |
| **Other bias** | Low risk | No evidence of other sources of bias. |

YYYStudy: Morgenstern 1998

# YYYMethods

Study design : parallel RCT. Total study duration : three years and six months (participant enrolment). Details of any 'run in' period : not reported. Number of study centres and location : single-centre: Hermann Hospital, USA. Date of study : May 1993 – October 1996 (participant enrolment).

Notes : the trial was prematurely stopped after three years as a result of slow patient accrual. During the total study duration, patients were simultaneously enroled in a prospective non-randomized (registry) study (n = 41) and a concurrent prospective RCT (n = 34). Early in this study patients were placed in the registry prior to initiation of the RCT months later. After the RCT began, patients were placed in the registry only if they refused randomisation or if the stroke team was not notified about the patient in time for randomisation.

# YYYParticipants

Number randomised: 35 (surgical group: 18; medical group: 17). Number lost to follow-up : 0. Number missing (exclusions & withdrawals) : 1 in surgical group (excluded due to randomisation of ineligible subject); none in medical group. Number analysed : 34 (surgical group: 17; medical group: 17). Number of cross-overs : 1 in the control group (reason not explicitly described, “..later had surgery"); none in the surgical group.

Baseline characteristics : median age 51 years (IQR 43 - 63) with range 22 - 77 years, male sex 65%, median GCS score 11 (IQR 10 - 14), median ICH volume 50 mL (IQR 30 - 76). ICH location: 24% lobar, 76% deep, 0% thalamic involvement (exclusion criterion). IVH extension not reported. There was a more frequent representation of deep ICH in the surgical group compared to the control group (94% vs. 59%, p=0.04), and a trend towards imbalance in time from onset to ER arrival (median 1.2 hours [range 0.25-9.1] in surgical group vs. 5.1 hours [range 1.1-10.5] in control group, p=0.06) and race (nonwhite 24% in surgical group vs. 41% in control group, p=0.06).

Inclusion criteria :

* Adult patients.

* Spontaneous supratentorial ICH >9 mL (lobar or deep extending outside the thalamus) diagnosed by head CT obtained <3 hours of screening.

* GCS score 5 – 15.

* Possibility to perform surgery <12 hours of documented symptom onset or last seen well.

Exclusion criteria :

* ICH secondary to known or suspected AVM, aneurysm, brain tumour or head trauma.

* Brainstem or cerebellar ICH, or ICH limited to the thalamus or ventricular system.

* Low level of function (Rankin score >2) prior to haemorrhage.

* Coagulopathy (PT >15 seconds, elevated PTT, platelet count <100 x 10 3 /mL) or current anticoagulant or thrombolytic use within the previous 24 hours.

* A serious pre-existing condition that, in the investigator’s judgement, increased surgical risk significantly or precluded 6-month survival.

* Biopsy-proved amyloid angiopathy.

* Haematoma volume of 10-19 mL and a GCS of 15, and better than antigravity strength on the affected side.

* Ventricular extension greater than ½ of one lateral ventricle or 1/3 of both lateral ventricles.

# YYYInterventions

Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. Patients in the surgical group underwent open craniotomy and haematoma evacuation. After the bone flap was turned and the dura was opened, a small cortical incision was made and, carefully, either through microscopic loops or a microscope or both, the clot was removed with the suction device only. No thrombolytic agents were used in any of the patients. When evacuation of the clot was completed, haemostasis was controlled with bipolar cautery and hydrogen peroxide-soaked cottonoids, which were subsequently removed. Thorough irrigation was performed of the haematoma bed, and no active bleeding was present at the time of dural closure and placement of the bone flap. The patients were returned to the neurologic ICU. Median time from symptom onset to surgery 8.3 hours (IQR not reported; range 3.75 - 26.1).

Standard medical management group : medical therapy was standardised between the two groups and supervised by a team of neurologists, neurosurgeons, and neuroanaesthesiologists in a dedicated neuroscience ICU. ICP monitors were placed in all patients with a GCS score < 9, and patients were treated with ventricular drainage, osmotic diuretics, sedation, paralysis, and hyperventilation as needed to maintain ICP < 21 cm H2O. IV steroids were not used. Blood pressure treatment was individualised for each patient depending on admission blood pressure.

Concomitant interventions : none.

# YYYOutcomes

Primary outcome : mortality at 1 month and 6 months. Secondary outcome : Barthel Index at 1 month and 6 months (“good functional outcome” defined as a Barthel Index of ≥61).

Note : mortality and the dichotomised BI at six months are only reported as percentages without the number of participants assessed, but we were able to find out the absolute numbers through contact with the study author. The BI at 1 month was also reported, however, not in a format suitable for meta-analysis (only as a median value instead of dichotomised).

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Random sequence generation (selection bias)** | Unclear risk | Details are not described in the paper, but the study author stated that random sequence generation was done by the study biostatistician using a computer program. Further details about the sequence generation approach are unknown to the study author. The study's biostatistician passed away. Therefore, there is insufficient information to assess whether the allocation sequence generation was adequate. |
| **Allocation concealment (selection bias)** | Low risk | The study author confirmed that sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes were used and opened only after the envelope had been assigned to the next enroled participant. Quote: “Randomization occurred using sealed, opaque envelopes with equal treatment allocation probabilities.” |
| **Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias) All outcomes** | High risk | Participants and local investigators were not blinded to treatment allocation. |
| **Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias) All outcomes** | High risk | Quote: “In this study, outcome was measured by an investigator unblinded to treatment allocation. Although this is a possible source of bias, structured interview was used to determine functional outcome for all patients.” |
| **Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias) All outcomes** | Low risk | One-post randomisation exclusion of an ineligible participant. Otherwise, outcome data is complete for the primary outcome. There are three missing values in the analysis of the Barthel Index at six months (reported as lost to follow-up, but the status of these participants was known to be alive). |
| **Selective reporting (reporting bias)** | High risk | All described outcomes in the methods are reported. However, mortality and the dichotomised functional outcome at six months are only reported as percentages without the number of participants assessed. We were able to find out the absolute numbers through contact with the study author. The reported results of the dichotomised functional outcome don’t correspond to the results of the corresponding definition of ‘poor outcomes’ described in the text (described as a Barthel Index of <61 or death, but the reported result are only based on the participants alive at 6 months, omitting the participants that died). |
| **Other bias** | Low risk | No evidence of other sources of bias. |

YYYStudy: Pantazis 2006

# YYYMethods

Study design : parallel RCT. Total study duration : one year (participant enrolment). Details of any 'run in' period : not reported. Number of study centres and location : single-centre: Thriassio hospital, Greece. Date of study : January 1998 – December 2003 (participant enrolment).

# YYYParticipants

Number randomised : not explicitly reported, only that “there were 108 patients diagnosed with primary subcortical or putaminal haemorrhage who fulfilled the study entry criteria”. Number lost to follow-up : not reported. Number missing (exclusions & withdrawals) : not reported. Number analysed : 108 (surgical group: 54; conservative group: 54). Number of cross-overs : 1 in the control group (neurological deterioration); none in the surgical group.

Baseline characteristics: mean age 61.4 years (SD 15.5) with range 31 - 80 years, male sex 56%, mean GCS score 8.8 (SD 4.7), mean ICH volume 56 mL (SD 24.5). ICH location: 47% lobar, 53% deep, 0% thalamic involvement (exclusion criterion), 52% left hemispheric. IVH extension not reported. No baseline imbalances between the surgical and standard medical management group.

Inclusion criteria :

* Spontaneous supratentorial ICH diagnosed by CT.

* ICH volume > 30 mL.

* Focal neurological deficit and/or impaired level of consciousness.

* Initiation of surgical or medical treatment <8 hours post-ictus.

Exclusion criteria :

* CT scan suggestive of underlying structural vascular abnormality, such as aneurysm or AVM, or an angiography finding positive for either of these entities.

* Age >80 years.

* Patients with thalamic haemorrhage.

* Patients with a GCS score of 15.

* Terminal medical illness

* Coagulopathy.

* Administration of anticoagulants.

* Trauma.

* Pregnancy.

* Lack of informed consent.

# YYYInterventions

Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. The surgical patients received the best medical treatment as well as surgery. Open craniotomy was performed with microscopic haematoma removal with a suction device. The clot was thoroughly evacuated, leaving only thin layers of coagulum adherent to particularly friable brain tissue. In most cases, satisfactory haemostasis was achieved with the use of cottonoids so that bipolar cauterisation of small blood vessels was rarely necessary. Epidural drains were routinely placed and the patients were returned to the ICU. Median time from symptom onset to surgery 7 hours (IQR 6 - 8).

Standard medical management group : best medical treatment without surgery. Decision on endotracheal intubation made early in emergency department and directed by respiratory failure. Initiation of antihypertensive treatment (reduction of hypertension by 20% from baseline) when SBP ≥180 mm Hg, DBP ≥105 mm Hg, or MAP ≥130 mm Hg; in emergency department with repeated intravenous boluses of short-acting agents, and steady control in the ICU with continuous infusions of antihypertensive agents. Emergency ICP control measures for comatose patients included optimal head positioning, mannitol administration, and hyperventilation to a PCO2 of 28-32 mm Hg. Initiation of invasive ICP monitoring in the ICU for patients with a GCS score ≤8, with a target CPP at 70-100 mm Hg. Initiation of hyperventilation to a pCO2 of 25-30 mmHg if ICP remained >20 mm Hg despite osmotherapy with mannitol. Aggressively lowering of elevated core body temperature using antipyretics with additional cooling blankets and ice when necessary. Isotonic fluids were administered as the standard intravenous replacement fluids. Enteral feeding commenced within 48 hours after ictus. Anticonvulsants (phenytoin or valproic acid) were given to reduce the risk of early seizures in patients with subcortical haematomas. In the absence of seizures, the prophylactic antiepileptic treatment was discontinued after 1 month. Therapy also included gastric cytoprotection, maintenance of normoglycemia, early nutritional support, and deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis with low-dose subcutaneous heparin started on day 2 after ictus. Physiotherapy was directed toward maintaining both limb mobility and pulmonary ventilation. Whenever possible, patients were taken out of bed and mobilised at the earliest reasonable time. Occupational therapy, speech therapy, and rehabilitation services were consulted as soon as medically feasible.

Concomitant interventions : none.

# YYYOutcomes

Mortality at 1 year; good functional outcome assessed with the GOS (GOS score >3) at 1 year.

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |

| **Random sequence generation (selection bias)** | Unclear risk | Insufficient information is provided to assess whether the allocation sequence generation was adequate, as the used sequence generation is incompletely defined and the use of some random component in the process is not confirmed. Quote: “The study statistician provided a list of random sequential assignment of cases to conservative or surgical treatment." |
| **Allocation concealment (selection bias)** | Unclear risk | Randomisation was conducted using envelopes. However, the minimal criteria for a judgement of adequate concealment of allocation sequence were not met as it is unclear whether the envelopes were also sequentially numbered, opaque and sealed. Quote: “Each patient assignment was placed in a numbered envelope, which was opened after signed informed consent has been obtained." |
| **Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias) All outcomes** | High risk | Participants and local investigators were not blinded to treatment allocation. |
| **Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias) All outcomes** | Unclear risk | Outcome assessments were performed by the physician investigator, who was not involved in the prior treatment of patients. It is unclear whether the physician investigator was blinded for treatment allocation. |
| **Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias) All outcomes** | Unclear risk | Only the number of “patients diagnosed with primary subcortical or putaminal haemorrhage who fulfilled the study entry criteria” is described. # YYYMethods

Study design : parallel RCT. Total study duration : five years and seven months (participant enrolment). Details of any 'run in' period : not reported. Number of study centres and location : multicentre: 129 neurosurgical units in 39 countries registered for participation. 78 centres in 27 countries randomly assigned patients (from North America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia). Date of study : January 11, 2007 – August 15, 2012 (participant enrolment).

# YYYParticipants

Number randomised : 601 (early surgery: 307; initial conservative treatment: 294). Number lost to follow-up : 3 (early surgery: 2, initial conservative treatment: 1). Number missing (exclusions & withdrawals) : overall 9; 7 in early surgery (2 excluded because recruited by centre that randomly assigned after haematoma evacuation; 5 withdrew); 2 in initial conservative treatment (excluded because recruited by centre that randomly assigned after haematoma evacuation). Number analysed: 597 (early surgery: 305; initial conservative treatment: 292). Number of cross-overs : 62 in the control group (36 deterioration in GCS; 1 oedema; 3 rebleed; 7 deterioration and oedema; 5 deterioration and rebleed; 4 deterioration, oedema and rebleed; 2 rise in ICP; 1 surgeon error; 2 family request, 1 underlying cause); 13 in the surgical group (6 families refused; 3 rebleed/intraventricular haemorrhage; 3 cardiac problem; respiratory problem or fever; 1 logistical problems).

Baseline characteristics : mean age 63.9 years (SD 13.3) with range 17 - 94 years, male sex 57%, median GCS score 13 (IQR 12 - 15), median ICH volume 36 mL (IQR 23.0 - 55.5). ICH location: 100% lobar (inclusion criterion), 0% deep, 0% thalamic involvement, 51% left hemispheric. IVH extension 0% (exclusion criterion). No baseline imbalances between the surgical and standard medical management group.

Inclusion criteria :

* Evidence of spontaneous lobar ICH on CT scan (≤1 cm from the cortical surface of the brain).

* ICH volume of 10 – 100 mL.

* Patient <48 hours of ictus.

* Best motor score on the GCS of 5 or 6 and best eye score on the GCS of 2 or more.

Exclusion criteria :

* Clear evidence that the haemorrhage is due to an aneurysm or angiographically proven AVM.

* ICH secondary to tumour or trauma.

* Haemorrhage involving the basal ganglia, thalamic, cerebellar, or brainstem regions.

* Any intraventricular blood;

* Severe pre-existing physical or mental disabilities or severe comorbidities that could interfere with the assessment of the outcome.

* If the haematological effects of any previous anticoagulants are not completely reversed.

# YYYInterventions

Surgical group : mixed surgical techniques (craniotomy: 99%; craniectomy: <1%; minimally invasive: 1% of which 2 burrhole with endoscopic evacuation and 1 keyhole evacuation). Early evacuation of the haematoma by the method preferred by the treating neurosurgeon, usually craniotomy, combined with appropriate best medical treatment. Surgeons were expected to endeavour to undertake evacuation of the haematomas within 12 hours of randomisation. Mean time from symptom onset to surgery 26.7 hours (SD 13.6).

Standard medical management group : best medical treatment as defined according to their hospital settings. Best medical treatment must begin as soon as possible and continue throughout follow-up, as required. Delayed evacuation was permitted if judged clinically appropriate.

Concomitant interventions : none.

# YYYOutcomes

Primary outcome : prognosis-based* favourable or unfavourable outcome dichotomised from the GOSE at 6 months (“favourable outcome” defined as a GOSE of 5-8 in the good prognosis group, and 4-8 in the poor prognosis group). Secondary outcomes : mortality; prognosis-based* dichotomised mRS at 6 months (“favourable outcome” defined as a mRS of ≤2 in the good prognosis group, and ≤3 in the poor prognosis group); GOSE at 6 months; mRS at 6 months; quality of life (reported as median) assessed with the EQ-5D-3L at 6 months.

* The prognosis-based outcome is a prognostic score based on GCS, age, and haemorrhage volume at randomisation. It was calculated as: 10×GCS−age−0.64×volume. The predefined cutoff of 27.672 for supratentorial ICH was used to divide the patients into a poor prognosis group and a good prognosis group.

Note : Dr. Gregson provided us with the following additional outcome data to include in our review: quality of life assessed with the mean EuroQol index at 6 months.

If it was necessary to administer these questionnaires to the patients then the interviewer was masked to treatment allocation. Outcome assignment, data cleaning, and CT assessment were all completed before the treatment assignment was unmasked. |

YYYStudy: Bhaskar 2017

# YYYMethods

Study design : parallel RCT. Total study duration : two years (participant enrolment). Details of any 'run in' period : not reported. Number of study centres and location : single-centre: King George’s Medical University, India. Date of study : September 2013 – August 2015 (participant enrolment).

Notes : target sample size was 80 participants.

# YYYParticipants

Number randomised : 61 (surgical management: 34; medical management: 27). Number lost to follow-up : none. Number missing (exclusions & withdrawals) : none. Number analysed : 61 (surgical management: 34; medical management: 27). Number of cross-overs : not reported.

Baseline characteristics : mean age 54.8 years (SD 5.7), male sex 61%, mean GCS score 6.8 (SD 2.3), mean ICH volume 64.6 mL (SD 18.0). ICH location: 15% lobar, 85% deep. IVH extension 51%. No baseline imbalances between the surgical and standard medical management group, besides a more frequent prevalence of hypertension in the surgical group (67.6% vs. 40.7%, p=0.036).

Inclusion criteria :

* Spontaneous supratentorial ICH.

* Age between 20–65 years.

* ICH volume on CT >30 mL.

* GCS score of 4–14.

* The symptoms appearing <72 hours prior to the diagnostic CT scan (an unknown time of symptom onset is exclusionary).

* Negative pregnancy test.

Exclusion criteria :

* Infratentorial extension of haemorrhage.

* Presence of coagulation disorders.

* Pregnancy or lactating females.

* Intra-tumoral haemorrhage.

* CT scan suspicion of haemorrhage due to cerebral aneurysm, AVM, or other vascular anomalies.

* Any concurrent serious illness that would interfere with the safety of the surgery.

# YYYInterventions

Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. The surgical management included a craniotomy, middle frontal gyrus approach, haematoma evacuation, and achievement of haemostasis. No thrombolytic agents were used in any of the patients. EVD was inserted if ventricles were exposed during the surgery, which was removed in 2–3 days or when CSF became clear. Average time from symptom onset to surgery not reported.

Standard medical management group : airway management, O2 by mask or ventilator support, head end elevation by 30°, hydration with input-output charting, control of blood pressure, reduction of ICP using mannitol and furosemide, prophylactic antiepileptic therapy to prevent seizures, prophylactic antibiotics, appropriate feeding, physiotherapy, and management of any associated morbidity, if present. All the patients were kept in the ICU with close monitoring of vital parameters and blood coagulation profile by a team consisting of neurosurgeons, neurophysicians, and critical care experts.

Concomitant interventions : none.

# YYYOutcomes

Primary outcome : mortality at 3 months. Secondary outcome : dependency assessed with the mRS at 3 months (“good functional outcome” defined as mRS ≤3).

plain_language_summary.S:
Does surgery for stroke due to bleeding in the brain improve the chance of people being able to function and live independently or cause any unwanted effects?

Key messages

• In adults with stroke due to bleeding in the brain, surgical removal of the bleeding may increase the chance of people being able to function independently and may reduce the risk of dying compared to people who are treated with standard medical care alone. We are very uncertain if surgical removal of the bleeding has an effect on quality of life after a stroke due to bleeding in the brain.

• It is uncertain if partial removal of the skull without removal of the bleeding has an effect on the ability to function independently, death, and quality of life after a brain haemorrhage, as there was only one study.

• More high-quality trials with more people with stroke due to bleeding in the brain are needed to find out if surgery is helpful and allow doctors to make recommendations for future clinical practice.

What is a brain haemorrhage and how is it treated?

Strokes that result from bleeding in the brain are known as brain haemorrhages. In about 20 in 100 people, the haemorrhage is caused by a problem with the structure of a blood vessel (abnormalities), trauma to the brain (for example, a blow to the head), or a brain tumour. In the remaining 80%, the haemorrhage results from damaged small blood vessels in the brain. Presently, there is no treatment that helps with brain haemorrhages, except the standard medical care provided in specialist stroke units, so-called 'bundled treatments' that rapidly correct physiological abnormalities, and possibly early control of high blood pressure. It is unknown whether surgery improves the function and lives of people with brain haemorrhages compared to standard medical care alone. Surgery for the treatment of brain haemorrhages includes:

• craniotomy (where a flap of bone is removed from the skull to access the brain) with removal of the bleeding;

• minimally invasive surgery (surgery through a small opening in the skull, with or without using a tube with a camera on it (called an endoscope), and with or without using medication to dissolve clotted blood); and

• partial removal of the skull without removal of the bleeding (which lowers the pressure in the brain and prevents further damage).

What did we want to find out?

We wanted to know if surgery improves or reduces the function and lives of people with brain haemorrhages compared to standard medical care alone. We were also interested in which surgical technique was best.

What did we do?

We searched for studies in adults with a brain haemorrhage that compared surgery plus standard medical care versus standard medical care alone. Studies could only investigate people with a brain haemorrhage that was not caused by an abnormality, trauma, or brain tumour. We compared and summarised the results of the studies and rated our confidence in the evidence, based on factors such as study methods and sizes.

What did we find?

We found 24 studies that involved 4597 people with a brain haemorrhage. Studies took place in Europe, North and South America, Asia, Africa, and Australia. The studies were published over a 35-year period from 1989 to 2024. Studies lasted for three to 12 months, with most studies lasting six months. Twenty-three studies looked at the surgical removal of brain haemorrhages, whereas one study looked at the partial removal of the skull without removal of the bleeding.

• Surgical removal of brain haemorrhages may increase the chance of being able to function independently and may reduce the risk of dying. It is unclear if surgical removal of the bleeding has an effect on quality of life after a brain haemorrhage.

• When the results were broken down by the surgical technique used to remove the bleeding, minimally invasive surgery may increase the chance of being able to function independently, but we are uncertain about this for craniotomy. However, surgical removal of the bleeding with craniotomy likely reduces the risk of death and minimally invasive surgery probably reduces the risk of death. Finally, craniotomy may make little to no difference to quality of life after a brain haemorrhage, while this is unclear for minimally invasive surgery.

• It is uncertain if partial removal of the skull without removal of the bleeding has an effect on the ability to function independently, death, and quality of life after a brain haemorrhage, as there was only one study.

What are the limitations of the evidence?

Our confidence in the evidence was moderate to very low. One important reason that lowered our confidence was how some studies were designed and conducted, which may have influenced the results. Also, some studies showed different results or only a limited number of people with a brain haemorrhage could be investigated, making the results less accurate.

How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is up to date to 11 March 2025.

YYYPlain language summary:

## Can vasodilators (medicines that widen blood vessels) help women with infertility have children?

### Key messages

1. Vasodilators (medicines that widen blood vessels) compared with dummy treatment or no treatment probably help women become pregnant, but probably have side effects. In addition, vasodilators compared with dummy treatment or no treatment, and compared with oestrogens (female sex hormones), may have little or no effect on the chance of women carrying the pregnancy to term and having the baby.
2. To draw more solid conclusions, we need larger, well-designed studies on this treatment.

### Background

For women undergoing fertility treatment, it is important to ensure the blastocyst (the rapidly dividing ball of cells that will become the fetus) can implant normally in the endometrium (womb lining). There are many medicines that could increase rates of implantation and live births. These include vasodilators, which dilate blood vessels to thicken the endometrium and help the womb relax, among other effects that could make the womb more receptive to the blastocyst.

### What did we want to find out?

We wanted to know whether vasodilators could help improve rates of live births, rates of pregnancy, and endometrial thickness. We also wanted to know whether vasodilators had any effect on rates of multiple pregnancy (twins, triplets, etc.), miscarriage, and ectopic pregnancy (when the fertilised egg implants outside the womb), and whether they had any side effects.

### What did we do?

We looked for studies comparing vasodilators with placebo (dummy treatment) or no treatment, or compared with a different medicine, in women of any age undergoing fertility treatment. We compared and summarised the results of the studies and rated our confidence in the evidence based on factors such as study size and methods.

### Study characteristics

We found 45 studies that compared vasodilators with placebo or no treatment or with oestrogens (one of the main female sex hormones) in a total of 4404 women undergoing fertility treatment. The studies were carried out in different countries: 20 in Egypt, 12 in Iran, four in Iraq, three in India, one in Australia, one in France, one in the UK, one in Russia, one in Belgium, and one in Korea. Only 21 of 45 studies declared the funding sources. Two of these studies declared financing was from pharmaceutical companies. Researchers or independent institutions funded the other 19 studies.

### Main results

#### Vasodilators compared with placebo or no treatment

Only six studies reported live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates in this comparison. Vasodilators compared with placebo or no treatment may have little or no effect on rates of live birth or ongoing pregnancy, but probably increase the chance of women becoming pregnant. Vasodilators probably have side effects, including headache and tachycardia (faster than normal heartbeat), but probably make little or no difference to rates of other unwanted events (multiple pregnancy, miscarriage, and ectopic pregnancy). We are unsure about the effect of vasodilators compared with placebo or no treatment on endometrial thickness.

#### Vasodilators compared with oestrogens

Only one study reported live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates in this comparison. Vasodilators compared with oestrogens may have little or no effect on rates of live birth or ongoing pregnancy, and we are unsure if they can help women become pregnant or improve endometrial thickness. The evidence on miscarriage is very uncertain.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

For the first comparison (vasodilators compared with placebo or no treatment), we are moderately confident in most of the evidence, but have less confidence in the results for live birth and endometrial thickness. For the second comparison (vasodilators compared with oestrogens), we are not confident in most of the evidence, and we have little confidence in the results for live birth. The main limitations of the evidence are that some studies were very small, many women knew which treatment they were receiving, and the results sometimes varied considerably from study to study.

More research is needed to draw more solid conclusions (13 studies are ongoing and will be incorporated into this review in a future update).

### How up to date is this evidence?

This review updates our previous review published in 2018. The evidence is current to April 2024.

plain_language_summary.S:
## Can vasodilators (medicines that widen blood vessels) help women with infertility have children?

### Key messages

1. Vasodilators (medicines that widen blood vessels) compared with dummy treatment or no treatment probably help women become pregnant, but probably have side effects. In addition, vasodilators compared with dummy treatment or no treatment, and compared with oestrogens (female sex hormones), may have little or no effect on the chance of women carrying the pregnancy to term and having the baby.
2. To draw more solid conclusions, we need larger, well-designed studies on this treatment.

### Background

For women undergoing fertility treatment, it is important to ensure the blastocyst (the rapidly dividing ball of cells that will become the fetus) can implant normally in the endometrium (womb lining). There are many medicines that could increase rates of implantation and live births. These include vasodilators, which dilate blood vessels to thicken the endometrium and help the womb relax, among other effects that could make the womb more receptive to the blastocyst.

### What did we want to find out?

We wanted to know whether vasodilators could help improve rates of live births, rates of pregnancy, and endometrial thickness. We also wanted to know whether vasodilators had any effect on rates of multiple pregnancy (twins, triplets, etc.), miscarriage, and ectopic pregnancy (when the fertilised egg implants outside the womb), and whether they had any side effects.

### What did we do?

We looked for studies comparing vasodilators with placebo (dummy treatment) or no treatment, or compared with a different medicine, in women of any age undergoing fertility treatment. We compared and summarised the results of the studies and rated our confidence in the evidence based on factors such as study size and methods.

### Study characteristics

We found 45 studies that compared vasodilators with placebo or no treatment or with oestrogens (one of the main female sex hormones) in a total of 4404 women undergoing fertility treatment. The studies were carried out in different countries: 20 in Egypt, 12 in Iran, four in Iraq, three in India, one in Australia, one in France, one in the UK, one in Russia, one in Belgium, and one in Korea. Only 21 of 45 studies declared the funding sources. Two of these studies declared financing was from pharmaceutical companies. Researchers or independent institutions funded the other 19 studies.

### Main results

#### Vasodilators compared with placebo or no treatment

Only six studies reported live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates in this comparison. Vasodilators compared with placebo or no treatment may have little or no effect on rates of live birth or ongoing pregnancy, but probably increase the chance of women becoming pregnant. Vasodilators probably have side effects, including headache and tachycardia (faster than normal heartbeat), but probably make little or no difference to rates of other unwanted events (multiple pregnancy, miscarriage, and ectopic pregnancy). We are unsure about the effect of vasodilators compared with placebo or no treatment on endometrial thickness.

#### Vasodilators compared with oestrogens

Only one study reported live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates in this comparison. Vasodilators compared with oestrogens may have little or no effect on rates of live birth or ongoing pregnancy, and we are unsure if they can help women become pregnant or improve endometrial thickness. The evidence on miscarriage is very uncertain.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

For the first comparison (vasodilators compared with placebo or no treatment), we are moderately confident in most of the evidence, but have less confidence in the results for live birth and endometrial thickness. For the second comparison (vasodilators compared with oestrogens), we are not confident in most of the evidence, and we have little confidence in the results for live birth. The main limitations of the evidence are that some studies were very small, many women knew which treatment they were receiving, and the results sometimes varied considerably from study to study.

More research is needed to draw more solid conclusions (13 studies are ongoing and will be incorporated into this review in a future update).

### How up to date is this evidence?

This review updates our previous review published in 2018. The evidence is current to April 2024.

YYYPlain language summary:

## Do trauma-dedicated hospital networks and trauma-dedicated hospitals improve outcomes for people with traumatic injuries?

### Key messages

* Due to a lack of robust evidence, we could not determine the benefits and unwanted effects of hospital networks (organised trauma systems) or individual hospitals (designated trauma centres) that are specialised in the care of people with traumatic injuries.
* This research calls for improvement in designing studies and reporting important measures such as death and survival, unwanted effects, use or access to trauma care services, quality of the care provided, providing care to everyone who needs it, and informing everyone about the care available.

### What are organised trauma systems, designated trauma centres, and usual care?

An organised trauma system is an entire service designed to provide care to injured people (for example, from road traffic collisions, weapons, and burns). It covers emergency and initial care at the location of the injury, transportation to the hospital, determining which hospital each patient is taken to, and care beyond their hospital stay. Trauma systems also include recovery of costs, overseas training, research, and injury prevention. Designated trauma centres are hospitals dedicated to treating people with traumatic injuries, and they form part of a trauma system network in a specific geographical location.

Trauma systems and trauma centres have been reported to offer a cost-effective approach to managing people with traumatic injuries in countries with a high standard of living. Evaluating its effectiveness by well-designed research is particularly important because this would support their use in resource-limited (poor) settings where the burden of injury is highest.

Usual care refers to general hospitals and healthcare systems that are not specifically dedicated to treating people with traumatic injuries. In regions or geographical locations where trauma systems have not been established, usual care is typically the standard approach.

### What did we want to find out?

We wanted to find out if organised trauma systems and designated trauma centres are:

* better than usual care for avoiding deaths and improving a person's recovery;
* associated with unwanted effects.

We specifically wanted to find their impact on:

* healthcare-related unwanted effects;
* use and access to health care;
* quality of the care provided;
* whether care was provided to everyone who needed it; and
* whether people knew what care was available.

### What did we do?

We searched for studies that investigated the effect of organised trauma systems and designated trauma centres compared to usual care. We were interested in deaths, unwanted effects, use or access to trauma care services, the quality of the care provided, providing care to everyone who needs it, and informing everyone about the care available.

We compared and summarised the results of the studies, and rated our confidence in the evidence based on factors such as study methods, and how precise and reliable the results were.

### What did we find?

We found four studies involving 157,111 people that evaluated the effectiveness of organised trauma systems or designated trauma centres. However, none of these studies were conducted in resource-limited countries.

We are not confident in the evidence because:

* there are insufficient studies to draw robust conclusions;
* the evidence did not comprehensively address all that we were interested in;
* some studies did not report data on what we were interested in;
* the studies varied in terms of the populations studied and the methods of delivering the care.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

Our confidence in the evidence is very low, and the results of further research could differ from the results of this review. The studies were not well designed, results were very inconsistent across the different studies, and they did not report all that we were interested in.

### How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is up to date to 16 December 2023.

# YYYMethods

| Characteristic    | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

| **Study design**  | Interrupted time series (ITS)                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Study centres** | The trauma network includes two level 1, four level 2 trauma centres, and seven non-trauma hospitals. In addition, there was a pre-hospital retrieval and treatment system coordinated by the level 1 trauma centres |

# YYYParticipants

| Characteristic          | Description                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Number**              | 20357 (11122 pre-intervention; 9235 post-intervention)                                                                                                                                            |
| **Age**                 | Mean 33 (pre-intervention) and 58 (post-intervention)                                                                                                                                             |

| **Exclusion criteria**  | Patients from neighbouring trauma systems or from hospitals outside the trauma network i.e., from counties that bordered multiple, different level 1 trauma centres (L1TC) excluded from analysis |

# YYYInterventions

**Intervention**

System-wide operational initiatives and protocols were developed and implemented in 2010. A single North Ohio Trauma System (NOTS) transfer line was created and housed in the L1TC to coordinate hospital transfers. A non-trauma hospital transfer/triage protocol was implemented according to patients' physiologic, anatomic, and mechanistic parameters. Shortly after, scene triage protocols were well implemented. Various NOTS committees were convened on a monthly basis, they included quality, protocol development, prevention, compliance, and network. In addition, a dedicated trauma intensive care unit (TICU), staffed by trauma/critical care attending physicians, was established at NOTS L1TC.

**Description of rationale, theory, or goal of essential elements to the intervention**

Traditional trauma systems were composed of single hospital systems that focused on the local need for trauma care. These systems failed to allocate resources based on patients' medical needs appropriately. A more recently inclusive regional trauma system incorporated medical centres within a geographical area with a hierarchical trauma level designation. Multiple studies performed outside the United States have shown that inclusive regional trauma systems can improve clinical and functional outcomes of adult and pediatric patients. Contrastingly, there was a scarcity of studies investigating the impact of these systems in the United States.

**Description of providers (background, expertise, training)**

The trauma departments and critical care units at level 1 trauma centres were staffed by trauma-trained physicians and critical-care providers.

**Mode of delivery of the intervention (face-to-face, by telephone, Internet)**

Direct clinical care.

**Description of location(s) infrastructure or relevant features of where intervention occurred**

The trauma network includes 2 level 1 and 4 level 2 trauma centres and seven non-trauma hospitals. In addition, a pre-hospital retrieval and treatment system coordinated by the level 1 trauma centres in North Ohio.

**How well was their intervention planned (if they assessed fidelity or adherence, describe how, by who, and if they employed strategies for maintaining fidelity)**

Limited descriptions of the physical infrastructure and how the intervention was implemented.

**How well was the intervention carried out, description of how the intervention adhered to the plan**

Not described.

# YYYOutcomes

Two analyses were done for the post-NOTS period:

1. A county analysis, comparing Cuyahoga County, the county containing NOTS L1TC, with other counties containing L1TCs.
2. A regional analysis, comparing the NOTS region with other Ohio regions with L1TC coverage.

Both the county and regional analyses showed the overall NOTS patients were 1 to 4 years older (p < 0.05), had similar or higher Injury Severity Score (p < 0.05), and were treated more often at lower-level TCs (p < 0.001). County analysis demonstrated that Cuyahoga County had approximately 1% lower mortality in geriatrics patients than non-NOTS counties. Regional analysis showed lower mortality in the NOTS region for the overall patient group and geriatric and blunt injuries subgroups. Cuyahoga was the only county that decreased mortality for both the general and groups over time (all p < 0.05).

**Outcome variables:** comparison of, demography (age/sex), treatment location (proportion of patients per TCs) and mechanism of injury (blunt, penetrating, burns, asphyxia), trauma incident per location and mortality.

characteristics_overall_notes.S: Extraction succeeded for all four studies using the attached **Supplementary material 2: Characteristics of included studies**. The supplement contains separate entries for Groven 2011, He 2016, Moran 2018, and Rotondo 2009. The text below preserves the terminology and wording of the characteristics table, with formatting converted to Markdown. The plain language summary was extracted from the main review PDF.

plain_language_summary.S:
## Do trauma-dedicated hospital networks and trauma-dedicated hospitals improve outcomes for people with traumatic injuries?

### Key messages

* Due to a lack of robust evidence, we could not determine the benefits and unwanted effects of hospital networks (organised trauma systems) or individual hospitals (designated trauma centres) that are specialised in the care of people with traumatic injuries.
* This research calls for improvement in designing studies and reporting important measures such as death and survival, unwanted effects, use or access to trauma care services, quality of the care provided, providing care to everyone who needs it, and informing everyone about the care available.

### What are organised trauma systems, designated trauma centres, and usual care?

An organised trauma system is an entire service designed to provide care to injured people (for example, from road traffic collisions, weapons, and burns). It covers emergency and initial care at the location of the injury, transportation to the hospital, determining which hospital each patient is taken to, and care beyond their hospital stay. Trauma systems also include recovery of costs, overseas training, research, and injury prevention. Designated trauma centres are hospitals dedicated to treating people with traumatic injuries, and they form part of a trauma system network in a specific geographical location.

Trauma systems and trauma centres have been reported to offer a cost-effective approach to managing people with traumatic injuries in countries with a high standard of living. Evaluating its effectiveness by well-designed research is particularly important because this would support their use in resource-limited (poor) settings where the burden of injury is highest.

Usual care refers to general hospitals and healthcare systems that are not specifically dedicated to treating people with traumatic injuries. In regions or geographical locations where trauma systems have not been established, usual care is typically the standard approach.

### What did we want to find out?

We wanted to find out if organised trauma systems and designated trauma centres are:

* better than usual care for avoiding deaths and improving a person's recovery;
* associated with unwanted effects.

We specifically wanted to find their impact on:

* healthcare-related unwanted effects;
* use and access to health care;
* quality of the care provided;
* whether care was provided to everyone who needed it; and
* whether people knew what care was available.

### What did we do?

We searched for studies that investigated the effect of organised trauma systems and designated trauma centres compared to usual care. We were interested in deaths, unwanted effects, use or access to trauma care services, the quality of the care provided, providing care to everyone who needs it, and informing everyone about the care available.

We compared and summarised the results of the studies, and rated our confidence in the evidence based on factors such as study methods, and how precise and reliable the results were.

### What did we find?

We found four studies involving 157,111 people that evaluated the effectiveness of organised trauma systems or designated trauma centres. However, none of these studies were conducted in resource-limited countries.

We are not confident in the evidence because:

* there are insufficient studies to draw robust conclusions;
* the evidence did not comprehensively address all that we were interested in;
* some studies did not report data on what we were interested in;
* the studies varied in terms of the populations studied and the methods of delivering the care.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

Our confidence in the evidence is very low, and the results of further research could differ from the results of this review. The studies were not well designed, results were very inconsistent across the different studies, and they did not report all that we were interested in.

### How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is up to date to 16 December 2023.

studies_overall_notes.S: The review does not contain forest plots for either outcome and reports that **zero studies were included in quantitative synthesis (meta-analysis)**. Instead, the individual interrupted time series results are presented narratively and in Tables 2 and 3. Consequently, no aggregated effect estimate, aggregated confidence interval, or conventional forest-plot analysis title is available. The review reports three related metrics for each analysis: relative effect, change in level, and change in slope. Because only change in level and change in slope have confidence intervals, the extraction below uses **change in level** as the effect measure. A value of 0.0 indicates no immediate change attributable to the intervention.

YYYPlain language summary:

## What are the benefits and risks of different human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines for preventing cervical cancer and other HPV-related disease?

### Key messages

HPV vaccination:

* reduces the incidence of cervical cancer by around 80% in people vaccinated at or before the age of 16 years;
* reduces the incidence of high-grade cervical pre-cancer lesions, as well as anogenital warts;
* is not associated with an increased risk of long-term side effects or infertility;
* is more effective when given at or before the age of 16 years, before onset of sexual activity.

### What is HPV?

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is transmitted between people through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal or oral sex. There are many types of HPV. Some types are harmless, but other types can cause cancer. Cervical cancer is the most common type of cancer that HPV can cause, but it can also cause vaginal, vulval, penile, anal, and head and neck cancer, as well as anogenital warts (a sexually transmitted infection caused by certain types of human papillomavirus). From the time of HPV infection, cervical cancer usually takes more than 10 years to develop, and other cancers take longer.

### How can HPV vaccines be beneficial?

In girls and boys, HPV vaccines aim to prevent HPV infection, which can sometimes cause cancer and anogenital warts. The HPV vaccines do not work well in people that have already been exposed to HPV. For this reason, most vaccination programmes aim to offer the vaccine to young people before they become sexually active.

### What did we want to find out?

We wanted more information on questions about long-term and rare outcomes that cannot be answered by randomised controlled trials (studies where people are assigned randomly to two or more treatment groups):

* What are the effects of introducing HPV vaccination on community rates of cervical, vaginal, vulval, anal and penile cancer, and the pre-cancerous stages of disease during the development of cancer?
* What are the effects of introducing HPV vaccination on the number of people who develop anogenital warts and the number of people who undergo treatment for HPV-related disease?

We also wanted to know if HPV vaccines were associated with any harmful effects, especially those discussed most frequently on social media.

### What did we do?

We searched for studies that evaluated the impact of HPV vaccination on population levels of cervical and other cancers, high-grade pre-cancer lesions (abnormal cell changes that occur after a persistent high-risk HPV infection and can develop into cancer if untreated), anogenital warts, treatment rates, HPV infections and unwanted or harmful (adverse) events. These included studies following groups of people after receiving HPV vaccination and studies observing the change in these diseases after national-level introduction of HPV vaccination.

We also searched social media sites (WebMD and X (formerly Twitter)) for commonly mentioned adverse events related to HPV vaccination. We searched for and included studies evaluating the impact of HPV vaccination on these events.

### What did we find?

We found 225 suitable studies from around the world that reported on the benefits and harms of HPV vaccination, including over 132 million people.

HPV vaccination probably reduces the incidence of cervical cancer by around 80% in people vaccinated at or before the age of 16 years. The reduction is lower for people vaccinated later.

HPV vaccination probably reduces the incidence of high-grade cervical pre-cancer lesions (CIN3+, CIN3, CIN2+ and CIN2), as well as anogenital warts. Again, reductions are greater in people who received the HPV vaccine at or before the age of 16 years.

There was lower-certainty evidence for the effect of HPV vaccination on rare diseases that take much longer to develop, such as adenocarcinoma in situ, other pre-cancer lesions and other cancers related to HPV (e.g. vaginal, vulval, anal and penile cancer). We identified fewer studies on these outcomes.

For most of the specific adverse events we looked at, including postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis, paralysis, complex regional pain syndrome, Guillain-Barré syndrome and infertility, there was moderate-certainty evidence that HPV vaccination likely does not increase the risk of developing them. HPV vaccination also did not increase sexual activity.

HPV vaccination also appears to reduce treatment rates associated with HPV disease, increases attendance at cervical screening programmes and reduces HPV infections.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

We are moderately confident in our results for cervical cancer, high-grade cervical disease, anogenital warts and specific harms. However, better and larger studies could show more reliable and precise results about the amount of protection.

### How up-to-date is this evidence?

The evidence is up-to-date to September 2024.

YYYOverall notes: The study characteristics and plain language summary are unchanged from the previous extraction. The YYYRisk of Bias sections have been replaced with outcome-specific judgements extracted directly from Figure 2, “Risk of bias by comparison and outcomes.” Figure 2 uses six domains because D2—bias arising from period and carryover effects—is applicable only to crossover trials; it is shown as not applicable for these parallel-group studies. Figure 2 does not provide written support for the individual domain judgements. 

YYYPlain language summary:

## What interventions improve adherence to amblyopia treatments in children?

### Key messages

* In general, none of the interventions reliably improved adherence to amblyopia treatment (specifically patching) in children. The interventions investigated also showed no evidence of improvement in vision or depth perception (judging how far away things are or ‘3-D vision’).
* Barriers to accessing treatments or appointments can impact how well children and their caregivers can carry out amblyopia treatment.
* More structured ways to track adherence are needed, as well as making reporting results about following treatment plans, vision, and depth perception more consistent.

### What is amblyopia?

Amblyopia is a technical term for reduced vision caused by abnormal visual development early in life. This results in not seeing as well with one or, less often, both eyes, even with optimal prescription eyeglasses or contact lenses. This is sometimes referred to as ‘lazy eye’ by parents and caregivers.

### What did we want to find out?

Adherence means how closely the amount of treatment completed matches the amount the healthcare provider prescribed. Adherence can be measured subjectively (e.g. by diary) or objectively (e.g. by sensing temperature contact with the skin). Examples of barriers to adherence include understanding the treatment, time, transportation, and availability or cost of the treatment or medical visits. We wanted to find out if any methods used to increase adherence to amblyopia treatment were successful and if any caused harm. In cases of amblyopia in one eye, treatment often consists of patching (covering or blocking) the better-seeing eye. This can be hard for children and their caregivers. Methods or interventions that we explored were behavioral, digital (i.e. technological or electronic, like playing a video game or watching a show), and different approaches to patching.

### What did we do?

We searched for studies that investigated: 1) a single or a combination of behavioral interventions, like educational cartoons and text message reminders; 2) digital stimulus interventions, like videos or video games; or 3) using different types of patches, like shutter glasses or different materials of patches, compared with the standard of care or no intervention (i.e. no method used to improve adherence).

### What did we find?

We found that most of the ways researchers tried to increase adherence were no different from each other. The evidence was uncertain, and so we were unable to draw conclusions that any one approach was better than any other.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

Few studies used objective tools to measure adherence. There was wide variation in the reporting of several characteristics and outcomes, including amblyopia severity, method of adherence monitoring, and follow-up duration, which had an impact on how confident we were in the evidence. Several outcomes related to adherence were not reported in each study and the clinical importance of the relative changes for these outcomes may vary by patient. Few studies assessed or reported on harms and factors related to fairness and inclusivity, such as socioeconomic status or caregiver education, with no standardization in reporting format.

### How up-to-date is this evidence?

The evidence is up-to-date to the search date of 24 May 2024.

plain_language_summary.S:
## What interventions improve adherence to amblyopia treatments in children?

### Key messages

* In general, none of the interventions reliably improved adherence to amblyopia treatment (specifically patching) in children. The interventions investigated also showed no evidence of improvement in vision or depth perception (judging how far away things are or ‘3-D vision’).
* Barriers to accessing treatments or appointments can impact how well children and their caregivers can carry out amblyopia treatment.
* More structured ways to track adherence are needed, as well as making reporting results about following treatment plans, vision, and depth perception more consistent.

### What is amblyopia?

Amblyopia is a technical term for reduced vision caused by abnormal visual development early in life. This results in not seeing as well with one or, less often, both eyes, even with optimal prescription eyeglasses or contact lenses. This is sometimes referred to as ‘lazy eye’ by parents and caregivers.

### What did we want to find out?

Adherence means how closely the amount of treatment completed matches the amount the healthcare provider prescribed. Adherence can be measured subjectively (e.g. by diary) or objectively (e.g. by sensing temperature contact with the skin). Examples of barriers to adherence include understanding the treatment, time, transportation, and availability or cost of the treatment or medical visits. We wanted to find out if any methods used to increase adherence to amblyopia treatment were successful and if any caused harm. In cases of amblyopia in one eye, treatment often consists of patching (covering or blocking) the better-seeing eye. This can be hard for children and their caregivers. Methods or interventions that we explored were behavioral, digital (i.e. technological or electronic, like playing a video game or watching a show), and different approaches to patching.

### What did we do?

We searched for studies that investigated: 1) a single or a combination of behavioral interventions, like educational cartoons and text message reminders; 2) digital stimulus interventions, like videos or video games; or 3) using different types of patches, like shutter glasses or different materials of patches, compared with the standard of care or no intervention (i.e. no method used to improve adherence).

### What did we find?

We found that most of the ways researchers tried to increase adherence were no different from each other. The evidence was uncertain, and so we were unable to draw conclusions that any one approach was better than any other.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

Few studies used objective tools to measure adherence. There was wide variation in the reporting of several characteristics and outcomes, including amblyopia severity, method of adherence monitoring, and follow-up duration, which had an impact on how confident we were in the evidence. Several outcomes related to adherence were not reported in each study and the clinical importance of the relative changes for these outcomes may vary by patient. Few studies assessed or reported on harms and factors related to fairness and inclusivity, such as socioeconomic status or caregiver education, with no standardization in reporting format.

### How up-to-date is this evidence?

The evidence is up-to-date to the search date of 24 May 2024.
