# YYYInterventions

Vaccination of patients and HCWs began October 1994 (“4 weeks before the earliest likely start date of the annual influenza outbreak”).

Parenteral influenza vaccine.

Vaccine strains probably matched the circulating strain.

* Serologically proven influenza (paired sera in 225 consenting patients in the “patients not vaccinated” arms).
* ILI, defined as a temperature of ≥ 37°C, “plus one of the following symptoms: new-onset cough, coryza, sore throat, malaise, headache, or muscle aches,” reported singly or within the ILI outcome and monitored from the end of October 1994 to the end of March 1995.
* LRTI “was identified by the presence of (1) pulmonary crackles, wheeze or tachypnoea plus temp ≥ 37°C or WBC > 10 × 10⁹/L or (2) a positive sputum culture” and was monitored from the end of October 1994 to the end of March 1995.
* Deaths from all causes.
* Deaths from pneumonia.
* All deaths and discharges and admissions to the wards were recorded.

* “Chest radiographs were not included as part of the routine assessment of suspected lower respiratory tract infection, as for many of the peripheral hospitals, it would have required an ambulance journey for the patient.”

# YYYMethods

| Characteristic           | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Purpose**              | To assess the effect of staff and resident influenza vaccination on resident all-cause mortality.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Design**               | C-RCT. A written invitation was sent to the 376 nursing homes with 50 to 200 elderly people (out of a total 1105 nursing homes) in the Paris area and 88 responded. Of these, 40 with staff influenza coverage < 40% during the 2005 to 2006 winter season were selected.                                                                     |
| **Matching**             | Each institution was pair-matched on size, staff vaccination coverage 2005 to 2006 and Group Iso Resources (GIR) weighted average disability score, which ranges from 1 = severe disability to 6 = total autonomy.                                                                                                                            |
| **Randomisation**        | Randomisation was centrally based using a random number generator.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Power assumptions**    | It was assumed that the influenza epidemic would last 2 months, mortality would be 8% in the control arm and resident mortality would be reduced 40% after staff vaccination to 4.8% in the intervention arm. 20 pairs of nursing homes with 2000 residents in each group were required to obtain 80% power with 2-tailed hypothesis testing. |
| **Analysis**             | Analysis was by intention-to-treat.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Statistical analysis** | “Odds ratios were calculated using alternating logistic regression, with one-nested log odds ratios to model the association between the responses of the same pair and the same nursing home within the pair.”                                                                                                                               |
| **Secondary analysis**   | “In secondary analyses, multivariate estimates were adjusted for the residents' age, vaccination status, GIR disability score and Charlson comorbidity index.”                                                                                                                                                                                |



# YYYParticipants

| Characteristic            | Description                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Country**               | France                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Setting**               | 40 nursing homes near Paris                                                                                                                                              |
| **Eligible participants** | 3483 patients in the 40 nursing homes                                                                                                                                    |
| **Intervention arm**      | 1592 residents at the beginning and 130 entered the homes during the study period (total = 1722); 989 staff were present at recruitment and 678 (68.6%) were vaccinated. |

# YYYInterventions

## Intervention

* Promotional campaign with posters, leaflets and an information meeting with the study team to sensitise staff to the benefits of influenza vaccination for oneself and residents.
* Face-to-face interviews with each member of staff present in nursing homes between 6 November and 15 December 2006.
* The study team met all administrative staff, technicians and caregivers to invite them to participate and those who volunteered were vaccinated at the end of the interview.
* The vaccine was inactivated Influvac (Solvay Pharma Laboratories), with 15 µG of each of:

  * A/Wisconsin/67/2005-like (H3N2)
  * A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1NH1)
  * B/Malaysia/2506/2004

## Control

Routine information on influenza vaccination.

## Primary

* All-cause mortality.

## Secondary

* Influenza, measured when clusters of ILI occurred in residents, using the Quick View Influenza Test.
* ILI, “defined as a fever of ≥ 37.8°C and onset of respiratory symptoms or worsening of chronic respiratory conditions.”

plain_language_summary.S:
## Flu vaccination for healthcare workers who care for people aged 60 or older living in long-term care institutions

### Key messages

Offering flu vaccination to people working in care institutions may make little or no difference to the number of residents who get flu or go to hospital with a chest infection, compared to those living in care institutions where no vaccination is offered.

Although we found that healthcare worker vaccination programmes led to fewer deaths due to any cause in residents of care institutions, we could not explain these results in terms of the reduction in flu or complications from chest infections.

### What is flu?

Flu is a respiratory illness. It is spread by a family of viruses and can affect people of all ages. Residents in long-term care institutions (LTCIs) are at a particularly high risk of being unwell with flu because their immune systems are weaker than people who live at home. People who work in LTCIs, such as doctors, nurses, other health professionals, cleaners and porters, may be exposed to flu during flu seasons. They often continue to work when they are infected with different respiratory viruses. This increases the likelihood of spreading them to those in their care. The signs and symptoms of flu are similar to those of many other respiratory illnesses. Therefore, it is important to test the effects of flu vaccination to prove by laboratory tests, which are highly accurate, whether residents in LTCIs actually have flu or another respiratory illness.

### What did we want to find out?

We wanted to know if vaccinating healthcare workers against flu reduces the risk of flu and its complications in older residents in LTCIs.

### What did we do?

We summarised existing research comparing different strategies to reduce flu in LTCIs. We looked for research studies which randomly assigned different care facilities to invite healthcare workers to receive flu vaccine at the start of the flu season or not.

### What did we find?

We identified four studies which included data from 8468 residents. Healthcare workers from care homes in France and the UK were randomly assigned to be offered a flu vaccination. The studies provided information on flu, chest infections, hospital admission for a chest infection, and death. We were unable to identify information about unwanted effects in the studies. The average age of the care home residents was between 77 and 86 years, and the majority were female (between 70% and 77%).

Offering flu vaccination to healthcare workers who care for those aged 60 or over in LTCIs may have little or no effect on flu. We have little confidence in the effects of healthcare worker vaccination programmes on the number of residents with chest infections or the number of residents admitted to hospital due to chest infections. We have very little confidence in the evidence for the number of residents who died from chest infections. Although the number of residents who died from any cause was lower after healthcare worker vaccination, a reduction from 9% to 6%, we could not explain this effect in terms of changes to the number of people with flu or complications from chest infection.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

We were mainly concerned about how people were followed up, the impact of people in the studies being aware of whether they were vaccinated, the use of interventions in the control groups, and low rates of vaccination in the studies. In two studies, data could not be included from everyone who was recruited and this reduced our confidence in the results from those studies. This review did not find information on other interventions used in conjunction with vaccination of healthcare workers (for example, hand washing, face masks, early detection of laboratory-proven flu, quarantine, avoiding new admissions, prompt antiviral use, asking healthcare workers with a flu-like illness not to go to work).

### How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is current to 22 August 2024.

YYYPlain language summary: Does giving a probiotic supplement to infants reduce allergies?

## Key messages

* Probiotics (live bacteria that provide health benefits to the digestive tract) given to newborns as a supplement or added to infant formula in the first six months of life may slightly reduce the development of eczema (dry, itchy and inflamed skin) in infants by the age of two years, but there are not enough good-quality studies to be certain about the result.
* Probiotics may have little to no effect on the development of allergic diseases such as asthma (a respiratory condition with symptoms like cough, wheezing, chest tightness and breathlessness) and allergic rhinitis (often called hay fever), and dietary allergies (to food and cow’s milk) during infancy.
* The effects of synbiotics (a mixture of probiotics and prebiotics (non-digestible fibres that help bacteria grow)) are uncertain.

## What are allergies?

Allergies to certain foods, such as cow’s milk, peanuts and eggs, as well as non-food allergies, are common. Some infants become sensitive to foods, including cow’s milk, through their digestive tract. This may be affected by the bacteria in the digestive tract. Other infants may become sensitive through the skin. Sensitisation to allergens (the component that causes the allergic reaction) tends to follow a pattern, with allergies to food occurring in the first two to three years of life, followed by indoor allergens (for example, house dust mites and pets) and subsequently outdoor allergens (for example, rye and Timothy grass) that present as asthma, eczema or allergic rhinitis.

## How can they be prevented?

Probiotics are helpful to the live gut bacteria that live in the digestive tract, and there is interest in whether probiotics might prevent sensitisation to allergens that lead to food allergies and non-food allergies.

## What did we do?

We wanted to find out the impact of giving probiotics or synbiotics (probiotics with added prebiotics (non-digestible fibres that help bacteria grow)) to infants in the first six months of life compared to giving a placebo (pretend treatment) or no treatment, on preventing the development of allergic diseases, including asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis, food allergy and cow’s milk allergy.

We searched for studies that gave infants probiotics or synbiotics as an intervention compared with no probiotics or synbiotics during the first six months of life. We compared and summarised the results of these studies and rated our confidence in the evidence, based on factors such as study methods and sizes.

## What did we find?

We included 24 studies that involved 7077 mother–infant pairs.

Probiotics may result in little to no difference in asthma, allergic rhinitis and cow’s milk allergy by two years of age. Probiotics may slightly reduce eczema by two years of age, but there were not enough good-quality studies for us to be certain about the result. Probiotics may have little to no effect on the occurrence of food allergy by two years of age, but the evidence is very uncertain.

The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of synbiotics on eczema by two years of age. Synbiotics may result in little to no difference in food allergy by two years of age. We found no data for the effect of synbiotics on asthma, allergic rhinitis and cow’s milk allergy by two years of age.

Probiotic or synbiotic supplementation may result in little to no difference in potential unwanted effects, including infection with probiotic bacteria by two years of age. There were no serious unwanted effects related to the use of probiotics or synbiotics reported.

## What are the limitations of the evidence?

We had some concerns about how some of the studies were conducted. Not all the studies provided data about everything that we were interested in. Most studies looked at probiotics and reported on eczema. There were not enough studies for us to be certain about the effects of probiotics and synbiotics on other allergic diseases and dietary allergies.

## How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is up to date to December 2023.  

YYYStudy: Allen 2014

# YYYMethods

Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group trial.

# YYYParticipants

**Inclusion criteria:** women 16 years or older with a normal singleton pregnancy. The intention was to recruit infants at high risk of developing atopy; however, sufficient details of atopy in first-degree relatives were often difficult to obtain at recruitment. Therefore, infants with and without increased risk of atopy were recruited.

**Exclusion criteria:** any known adverse condition affecting the woman, foetus, or the likely outcome of the pregnancy; if a member of the foetus’s sibship or household was already recruited to the study; or if the woman was unwilling to discontinue use of other live bacterial dietary supplements.

# YYYInterventions

* **Treatment (n = 220):** probiotic supplement *Lactobacillus salivarius* LS33 6.25 × 10⁹ cfu, *Lactobacillus paracasei* CUL08 1.25 × 10⁹ cfu, *Bifidobacterium infantis* Bi07 1.25 × 10⁹ cfu and *Bifidobacterium bifidum* CUL20 1.25 × 10⁹ cfu.
* **Control (n = 234):** maltodextrin 100 mg.
* Mother from 36 weeks’ gestation until delivery. Infant from birth to 6 months.
* Weeks (median (range)) exclusively breast-fed, treatment group (n = 167): 2 (0–8); control (n = 161): 3 (0–8).
* Both arms received 1 capsule daily from 36 weeks’ gestation until delivery. Infants received the same capsules as their mother 1× daily from birth to age 6 months. Contents of the capsule were sprinkled directly into the infant’s open mouth or mixed with expressed breast milk or formula feed.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcomes:** the cumulative frequency of diagnosed eczema (assessed by the SCORAD system) at the 2-year follow up (reported by a parent to have been diagnosed by a clinician or assessed by a study clinician or trained research personnel). Changes to symptoms and adverse effects related to atopy.
* **Other outcomes:** responses to SPTs, atopic eczema defined as eczema with 1 or more positive SPTs, eczema of any duration and whether or not diagnosed by health professional, severity of eczema, treatment with topical steroid preparations, respiratory symptoms with asthma and allergic rhinitis and reported food allergies.
* **Definition:** eczema defined as an itchy rash affecting the face, scalp or extensor surfaces of the limbs in infants and flexures in older children and of duration ≥ 4 weeks and with ≥ 1 exacerbation by age 24 months. 

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                            | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Bias arising from the randomisation process**        | Low risk           | Randomisation was conducted using a computer-generated randomisation code, with treatment allocation performed independently. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups.                                |
| **Bias due to deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk           | Participants and trial personnel were blinded. The analysis was appropriate for estimating the effect of assignment to intervention, and there was no evidence that deviations arose because of the trial context. |
| **Bias due to missing outcome data**                   | Low risk           | Outcome data were available for a sufficient proportion of randomised participants, and missingness was not considered likely to depend on the true outcome value.                                                 |
| **Bias in measurement of the outcome**                 | Some concerns      | There was potential recall bias and delayed follow-up in children seen up to, but not including, three years of age.                                                                                               |
| **Bias in selection of the reported result**           | Some concerns      | A prespecified analysis plan was not available.                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Overall bias**                                       | Some concerns      | The study raised some concerns because of the assessments for measurement of the outcome and selection of the reported result.                                                                                     |

The review specifically identifies Allen 2014 as having some concerns for outcome measurement because of potential recall bias and delayed follow-up, and as having some concerns for selective reporting because no prespecified analysis plan was available. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][1])

YYYStudy: Plummer 2020

# YYYMethods

Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial.

# YYYParticipants

**Inclusion criteria:** preterm infants both below 1500 g and less than 32 weeks’ gestational age at birth.

**Exclusion criteria:** infants suspected of or has major congenital anomalies, considered likely to die within 72 hours of birth as excluded. Babies of mothers who are already taking supplemental probiotics by capsule (not yogurt, etc) are excluded.

# YYYInterventions

* **Treatment (n = 548):** 1 × 10⁹ total organisms per 1.5 gm *Bifidobacterium infantis*, *Streptococcus thermophilus* and *Bifidobacterium lactis* (“ABC Dophilus Probiotic Powder for Infants®”, Solgar, USA) is given to infants from soon after the start of milk feeds until discharge home or term corrected, whichever comes first.
* **Control (n = 511):** placebo. Maltodextrin powder contains 4 kcal/gram and is dairy free, gluten-free and suitable for vegans. The daily dose is 1.5 g of study powder, irrespective of infant’s weight or postnatal age.
* Substudy in Victorian participants (n = 683) at 12 months’ corrected age. Of the participants analysed in the substudy, probiotic group n = 127, placebo group n = 154.
* The study intervention or placebo was given orally or via gastric tube once daily, unless the feed volume is less than 3 mL when 1 level ProPrems trial measuring spoon of powder is administered in 1.5 mL feed twice daily. Freshly expressed mother’s breast milk is the feed of choice, followed by frozen breast milk, if fresh is not available. Banked breast milk is used when mother’s milk is not available in centres with established protocols that use breast milk banking. Formula is used only when there is insufficient breast milk or if the mother chooses not to provide breast milk. Tube feeding is commenced as soon as possible in small and increasing amounts according to local protocols and the discretion of the treating neonatalist. Intravenous fluids and nutrition are used until approximately 120 ml/kg of milk is tolerated per 24-hour period.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcome:** incidence of at least 1 episode of definite late onset sepsis before 40 weeks’ corrected age or discharge home.
* **Secondary outcomes:** incidence of clinically-suspected sepsis, NEC, mortality, duration of primary hospital admission, number of courses of antibiotics, number of days until full enteral feeds established.
* **Substudy outcomes:** growth, infections, hospital admissions and antibiotic courses, cumulative incidence of allergic disease, immunological parameters, allergic sensitisation at 12 months.
* **Definitions:** eczema was defined as parent report of doctor diagnosis of eczema or fulfillment of the modified UK Working Party’s Diagnostic Criteria (William 1994), for atopic dermatitis; a history of itchy skin in the preceding 12 months, plus ≥ 3 of the following visible dermatitis involving the skin creases extensor surfaces or cheeks, or both; a history of generally dry skin in the preceding 12 months; and a history of asthma or allergic rhinitis (or history of atopic disease in a first-degree relative).
* Atopic eczema was defined as eczema together with a positive SPT to 1 or more allergen.
* Food allergy was defined as parent report of doctor-diagnosed cow’s milk, soy, egg, wheat, or peanut allergy with or without a positive SPT to the relevant food allergen to capture both IgE and non-IgE–mediated food allergy phenotypes.
* Wheeze was defined as any parental reported wheeze, and number of infections during the first 2 years of life was defined as parent-reported number of colds with fever lasting at least 3 days to ensure medically significant infections were captured. 

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                            | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bias arising from the randomisation process**        | Low risk           | The allocation sequence was generated centrally, and the intervention and placebo groups were generally balanced following randomisation.                                                                                                                            |
| **Bias due to deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk           | Infants, families, clinical staff and outcome assessors were blinded to treatment allocation. There was no evidence of intervention-related deviations that would affect the intention-to-treat effect.                                                              |
| **Bias due to missing outcome data**                   | Some concerns      | Only the Victorian substudy participants were assessed for allergic disease. Among participants analysed in the substudy, 127 probiotic-group infants and 154 placebo-group infants contributed data. The review judged missing outcome data to raise some concerns. |
| **Bias in measurement of the outcome**                 | Low risk           | Food allergy was defined using parent report of a doctor diagnosis, with or without a positive skin-prick test to the relevant food allergen. Measurement methods were applied similarly across groups.                                                              |
| **Bias in selection of the reported result**           | Low risk           | The reported result was considered consistent with the prespecified trial and substudy outcomes.                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Overall bias**                                       | Some concerns      | The overall assessment reflected concerns about missing outcome data in the allergic-disease substudy.                                                                                                                                                               |

The review’s general assessment identifies Plummer 2020 among studies raising concerns because of missing outcome data, while it is not among the studies identified as having concerns about randomisation, outcome measurement, or selection of the reported result. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][1])

YYYStudy: Taylor 2006

# YYYMethods

Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.

# YYYParticipants

**Inclusion criteria:** pregnant, atopic women. Maternal atopy defined as doctor-diagnosed clinical history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or eczema plus a positive SPT to 1 or more common allergens.

**Exclusion criteria:** women excluded if smoked, had other medical problems or pregnancy complications, delivered before 37 weeks’ gestation, or already taking probiotic supplements.

# YYYInterventions

* **Treatment (n = 115):** 3 × 10⁹/L *L. acidophilus* LAVRI-A1 in maltodextrin (Probiomics, Sydney, Australia). Supplements supplied as stable freeze-dried powder, dissolved in 1 to 2 mL sterile water and administered orally daily from birth to 6 months.
* **Control (n = 111):** maltodextrin alone.
* Intervention commenced within 48 hours of delivery and was given only to the baby, independent of feeding method.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcomes:** clinical assessment of atopic dermatitis at 6 and 12 months of age. Incidence of atopic dermatitis, food allergy, and sensitisation at 12 months and 2.5 years of age. Primary allergy prevention in a population of Australian children at high risk of allergic disease.
* **Other outcomes:** detailed history and examination collected at 12 months and 2.5 years by the same paediatric allergist. Other symptoms based on parental record; all parents who noted “noisy breathing” of any kind were asked to give detailed descriptions of this to the paediatrician. Doctor-diagnosed gastrointestinal infections were recorded. Assessment of the expression of T-regulatory phenotype.
* **Atopic dermatitis:** typical skin lesions responsive to topical steroids. The severity determined using the severity score of atopic dermatitis (SCORAD).
* **IgE-mediated food allergy:** history of immediate symptoms after contact with or ingestion of food and a positive SPT to the implicated food. Symptoms of acute food allergy include skin reactions (hives, rash or swelling) or respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze, stridor) or gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain, vomiting, loose stools) or cardiovascular symptoms (collapse).
* **Asthma:** defined as recurrent wheezing (3 or more episodes, at least 1 confirmed by a paediatrician or general practitioner) with evidence of responsiveness to bronchodilator therapy. 

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                            | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bias arising from the randomisation process**        | Some concerns      | There were significant differences in birth length and birth head circumference between the groups analysed.                                                                                                                                          |
| **Bias due to deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk           | Participants, carers and trial personnel were blinded. Intervention was administered independently of feeding method, and there was no evidence of important deviations caused by the trial context.                                                  |
| **Bias due to missing outcome data**                   | Low risk           | For the infant food-allergy outcome, missing data were not considered sufficient to place the result at serious risk of bias. The review’s concern about substantial loss to follow-up applied to the later five-year childhood-incidence assessment. |
| **Bias in measurement of the outcome**                 | Low risk           | Food allergy required a history of immediate symptoms following food exposure and a positive skin-prick test to the implicated food. Assessment was conducted by the same paediatric allergist.                                                       |
| **Bias in selection of the reported result**           | Some concerns      | A prespecified analysis plan was not available.                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Overall bias**                                       | Some concerns      | The assessment reflected concerns about the randomisation process and selection of the reported result.                                                                                                                                               |

The review directly attributes some concerns in the randomisation domain to significant differences in birth length and head circumference, and identifies Taylor 2006 among studies lacking an available prespecified analysis plan. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][1])

YYYStudy: Dissanayake 2018

# YYYMethods

2 × 2 factorial, randomised, non-treatment controlled trial.

# YYYParticipants

**Inclusion criteria:** families who attended the antenatal clinic were recruited into the study. Following delivery, the babies were recruited if they were born at term and written informed consent was available from parent(s)/guardian. A family history of atopy was not required for inclusion.

**Exclusion criteria:** infants born pre-term, experience complications due to severe underlying disease were excluded from the study. HBV or HIV positivity of mother at the time of birth or any other inappropriate status as judged by the physician.

# YYYInterventions

* **Synbiotic and skincare (n = 137):** combination of 0.5 g (7 × 10⁹ CFU/g) of *Bifidobacterium bifidum* OLB6378 (Meiji Holdings Co. Ltd., Japan) combined with 0.5 g of fructo-oligosaccharides (Meiji Food Materia Co., Ltd., Japan) twice a day and Locobase® REPAIR Cream (Daiichi Sankyo, Japan), which contains ceramide, cholesterol, and free fatty acids, 2–3 times a day. Intervention was carried out from birth to 6 months of age.
* **Synbiotic only (n = 137):** combination of 0.5 g (7 × 10⁹ CFU/g) of *Bifidobacterium bifidum* OLB6378 (Meiji Holdings Co. Ltd., Japan) combined with 0.5 g of fructo-oligosaccharides (Meiji Food Materia Co., Ltd., Japan) 2× a day from birth to 6 months of age.
* **Skincare only (n = 138):** Locobase® REPAIR Cream (Daiichi Sankyo, Japan), which contains ceramide, cholesterol, and free fatty acids, 2–3 times a day from birth to 6 months.
* **Control (n = 137):** the control group did not receive any synbiotics. The no-treatment group was not prevented from applying emollients due to ethical reasons.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcome:** development of atopic dermatitis by 1 year of age.
* **Secondary outcome:** prevalence of food allergy. Sensitisation to food or inhalant allergens or both. EASI score examined by a paediatrician.
* **Definitions:** atopic dermatitis was diagnosed according to the criteria of the Japanese Dermatological Association (Katayama 2017), and using the UK Working Party’s Diagnostic Criteria (William 1994), included in the questionnaire at 1 year. Defined as itchy rash lasting 2 or more months was reported in the questionnaires returned at 1, 6, and 9 months and 1 year of the baby’s age.
* Food allergy reported in the questionnaire at 1 year. Sensitisation to food or inhalant allergens in total, or both, and allergen-specific IgE levels in blood sampled at 9 months of age. 

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                            | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bias arising from the randomisation process**        | Low risk           | A computer-generated randomisation sequence was used for the 2 × 2 factorial allocation. There was no indication that the allocation sequence was compromised.                                                                    |
| **Bias due to deviations from intended interventions** | Some concerns      | The study used a no-treatment control group. Participants and carers were therefore aware of whether synbiotic treatment was received, and the no-treatment group was not prevented from applying emollients for ethical reasons. |
| **Bias due to missing outcome data**                   | Low risk           | Outcome data were available for a sufficient proportion of participants, and missingness was not considered likely to depend on the true eczema outcome.                                                                          |
| **Bias in measurement of the outcome**                 | Low risk           | Atopic dermatitis was assessed according to the Japanese Dermatological Association and UK Working Party diagnostic criteria, with EASI examination by a paediatrician.                                                           |
| **Bias in selection of the reported result**           | Some concerns      | A prespecified analysis plan was not available.                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Overall bias**                                       | Some concerns      | The assessment reflected concerns about deviations from intended interventions and selection of the reported result.                                                                                                              |

The review notes that Dissanayake 2018 used no treatment as its comparator and identifies it among studies for which no prespecified analysis plan was available. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][1])

YYYStudy: Kukkonen 2006

# YYYMethods

Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.

# YYYParticipants

**Inclusion criteria:** pregnant women with at least 1 parent of the unborn child had a physician-diagnosed allergic disease.

**Exclusion criteria:** infants born < 37 weeks’ gestation, infants with major malformations, and B-twins.

# YYYInterventions

* **Treatment (n = 610):** mothers took 1 capsule for 2–4 weeks before delivery containing *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* GG (ATCC 53103), 5 × 10⁹ cfu; *L. rhamnosus* LC705 (DSM 7061), 5 × 10⁹ cfu; *Bifidobacterium breve* Bb99 (DSM 13692), 2 × 10⁸ cfu; and *Propionibacterium freudenreichii* ssp. *shermanii* JS (DSM 7076), 2 × 10⁹ cfu. Their newborn infants received 1 opened capsule containing the same probiotic mixed with 20 drops of sugar syrup containing 0.8 g of galacto-oligosaccharides once daily for 6 months after birth.
* **Control (n = 613):** placebo group mothers and infants took capsules containing microcrystalline cellulose, and infants received sugar syrup without galacto-oligosaccharides.
* Exclusive breast-fed treatment group 2.6 months, control group 2.4 months. Standard adapted cow’s milk-based formula replaced breast milk when breast-feeding was insufficient. The use of hypoallergenic formula was restricted to infants allergic to cow’s milk.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcomes:** any allergic disease (food allergy, eczema, asthma, and allergic rhinitis) and IgE-associated (atopic) disease at 2 years.
* **Other outcomes:** eczema and sensitisation. Physician assessment at 3, 6, 24 months and 5 years. At 10 years parents completed questionnaires based on the ISAAC study. At 13 years, follow-up questionnaire was completed.
* **Food allergy:** diagnosed with an open food challenge.
* **Eczema:** according to the UK Working Party’s criteria (an itchy skin condition plus ≥ 3 of atopic disease in the family, dry skin during the last year, history of eczema, or visible eczema involving typical sites), (William 1994).
* **Atopic eczema:** if IgE associated.
* **Severity of eczema:** evaluated using SCORAD score.
* **Asthma:** 2 or more physician-diagnosed wheezing episodes accompanied by persistent cough or exercise-induced symptoms. 

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                            | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bias arising from the randomisation process**        | Low risk           | The allocation sequence was computer-generated and stratified, and baseline characteristics did not indicate an important randomisation problem.                                                                       |
| **Bias due to deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk           | Mothers, families, investigators and outcome assessors were blinded through use of matching placebo capsules and syrup. There was no evidence of important deviations related to knowledge of intervention assignment. |
| **Bias due to missing outcome data**                   | Low risk           | Outcome data for eczema by two years were available for a sufficient proportion of participants, and missingness was not judged likely to depend on the true outcome.                                                  |
| **Bias in measurement of the outcome**                 | Low risk           | Eczema was assessed by physicians using the UK Working Party criteria, and severity was evaluated using the SCORAD score.                                                                                              |
| **Bias in selection of the reported result**           | Some concerns      | A prespecified analysis plan was not available.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Overall bias**                                       | Some concerns      | The overall assessment reflected concern about selection of the reported result.                                                                                                                                       |

Kukkonen 2006 is among the studies the review identifies as having some concerns in the selective-reporting domain because a prespecified analysis plan was unavailable. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][1])

YYYStudy: Rozé 2012

# YYYMethods

Double-blind randomised controlled trial.

# YYYParticipants

**Inclusion criteria:** gestational age > 37 weeks, a postnatal age less than 3 days, fed from birth with probiotic- and prebiotic-free infant formula, and without human milk before inclusion. 4 centres participated in the trial (Mother-and-Children Hospital, Nantes, France; Children’s Hospital Angers, France; Hospital Saint-Vincent de Paul and Hospital Salpêtrière, Paris, France).

**Exclusion criteria:** infant presenting a metabolic, nervous, digestive or organic disease able to interfere with study, evidence of cow’s milk protein allergy, infant presenting lactose intolerance.

# YYYInterventions

* **Treatment (n = 48):** the experimental formula was characterised by the presence of 2 strains of probiotics (*Lactobacillus rhamnosus* LCS-742 and *Bifidobacterium longum* subsp. *infantis* M63) and by the addition of prebiotics: 96% galacto-oligosaccharides and 4% short-chain fructo-oligosaccharides. This formula was also enriched with bovine α-lactalbumin, using a native whey protein concentrate with high α-lactalbumin concentration (34% of soluble proteins) obtained using careful fractionation techniques (ultrafiltration).
* **Control (n = 49):** standard infant formula.
* The intervention ended at 6 months of age.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcomes:** anthropometric measurements such as weight, length, BMI, and cranial perimeter. Dermatological examination and scoring atopic dermatitis (SCORAD) index calculation, sleeping time and general well-being using structured interviews.
* **Other outcomes:** formula intake for each meal, bowel habits and stool consistency over the 3 days before each visit were also collected from a home diary kept by the parents.
* **Definitions:** atopic dermatitis utilised the UK Working Party’s diagnostic criteria (William 1994), and SCORAD index was calculated to assess severity. 

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                            | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bias arising from the randomisation process**        | Some concerns      | The allocation-concealment method or random-sequence-generation process was not adequately described.                                                                                                            |
| **Bias due to deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk           | The study was double-blind, and the intervention and control formulas were administered according to the assigned groups. There was no evidence of important deviations caused by knowledge of assignment.       |
| **Bias due to missing outcome data**                   | Some concerns      | The study did not report whether dropouts were related to the eczema outcome or provide sufficient information to establish that missingness was unrelated to the true outcome.                                  |
| **Bias in measurement of the outcome**                 | Low risk           | Atopic dermatitis was assessed using the UK Working Party diagnostic criteria, and severity was measured using the SCORAD index.                                                                                 |
| **Bias in selection of the reported result**           | Some concerns      | A prespecified analysis plan was not available.                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Overall bias**                                       | High risk          | Multiple domains raised concerns, including the randomisation process, missing outcome data, and selection of the reported result. The review’s forest plot classified the study’s overall risk of bias as high. |

The review identifies Rozé 2012 as having inadequately described randomisation or allocation concealment, concerns about missing outcome data, and no available prespecified analysis plan. Its eczema forest plot shows an overall high-risk judgement. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][1])

plain_language_summary.S:
Does giving a probiotic supplement to infants reduce allergies?

## Key messages

* Probiotics (live bacteria that provide health benefits to the digestive tract) given to newborns as a supplement or added to infant formula in the first six months of life may slightly reduce the development of eczema (dry, itchy and inflamed skin) in infants by the age of two years, but there are not enough good-quality studies to be certain about the result.
* Probiotics may have little to no effect on the development of allergic diseases such as asthma (a respiratory condition with symptoms like cough, wheezing, chest tightness and breathlessness) and allergic rhinitis (often called hay fever), and dietary allergies (to food and cow’s milk) during infancy.
* The effects of synbiotics (a mixture of probiotics and prebiotics (non-digestible fibres that help bacteria grow)) are uncertain.

## What are allergies?

Allergies to certain foods, such as cow’s milk, peanuts and eggs, as well as non-food allergies, are common. Some infants become sensitive to foods, including cow’s milk, through their digestive tract. This may be affected by the bacteria in the digestive tract. Other infants may become sensitive through the skin. Sensitisation to allergens (the component that causes the allergic reaction) tends to follow a pattern, with allergies to food occurring in the first two to three years of life, followed by indoor allergens (for example, house dust mites and pets) and subsequently outdoor allergens (for example, rye and Timothy grass) that present as asthma, eczema or allergic rhinitis.

## How can they be prevented?

Probiotics are helpful to the live gut bacteria that live in the digestive tract, and there is interest in whether probiotics might prevent sensitisation to allergens that lead to food allergies and non-food allergies.

## What did we do?

We wanted to find out the impact of giving probiotics or synbiotics (probiotics with added prebiotics (non-digestible fibres that help bacteria grow)) to infants in the first six months of life compared to giving a placebo (pretend treatment) or no treatment, on preventing the development of allergic diseases, including asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis, food allergy and cow’s milk allergy.

We searched for studies that gave infants probiotics or synbiotics as an intervention compared with no probiotics or synbiotics during the first six months of life. We compared and summarised the results of these studies and rated our confidence in the evidence, based on factors such as study methods and sizes.

## What did we find?

We included 24 studies that involved 7077 mother–infant pairs.

Probiotics may result in little to no difference in asthma, allergic rhinitis and cow’s milk allergy by two years of age. Probiotics may slightly reduce eczema by two years of age, but there were not enough good-quality studies for us to be certain about the result. Probiotics may have little to no effect on the occurrence of food allergy by two years of age, but the evidence is very uncertain.

The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of synbiotics on eczema by two years of age. Synbiotics may result in little to no difference in food allergy by two years of age. We found no data for the effect of synbiotics on asthma, allergic rhinitis and cow’s milk allergy by two years of age.

Probiotic or synbiotic supplementation may result in little to no difference in potential unwanted effects, including infection with probiotic bacteria by two years of age. There were no serious unwanted effects related to the use of probiotics or synbiotics reported.

## What are the limitations of the evidence?

We had some concerns about how some of the studies were conducted. Not all the studies provided data about everything that we were interested in. Most studies looked at probiotics and reported on eczema. There were not enough studies for us to be certain about the effects of probiotics and synbiotics on other allergic diseases and dietary allergies.

## How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is up to date to December 2023.

The text below preserves the terminology and wording of the supplementary characteristics table; the Identification and Notes fields were omitted as requested.

YYYPlain language summary: What are the benefits and risks of different ways of accessing the hip joint during partial hip replacement surgery?

## Key messages

* The evidence is still developing, and future studies may change our conclusions.
* We are not confident that one surgical approach (way of accessing the hip joint) compared to another leads to a different outcome for performing daily tasks, health-related quality of life, mobility or functional status, mortality, or pain, within the first four months after surgery.

## What is hip hemiarthroplasty?

Hip hemiarthroplasty, or partial hip replacement, is surgery that replaces the ball of the thighbone (femur) with an artificial one, leaving the socket untouched.

## Why is this important for people with hip fractures?

Hip fractures are common, especially in older adults. They can be very painful and make it hard to walk or live independently. Partial hip replacement is a way to fix these fractures, reducing pain, and getting people back on their feet faster. There are different ways to access the hip joint during surgery (approaches). Each has its own benefits and drawbacks.

## What did we want to find out?

We wanted to find out what effect different surgical approaches for performing a partial hip replacement can have on a person recovering from surgery.

## What did we do?

We searched for studies comparing different approaches for partial hip replacement. Studies had to choose people at random (or use their dates of birth or alternate methods) for each approach and then follow their recovery after surgery. Studies included adults with hip fractures. We compared and summarised the study results, and rated our confidence in the evidence, based on factors such as study size and methods.

## What did we find?

We found 27 studies with 3369 people. Studies took place throughout Europe and Asia. The biggest study had 843 people and the smallest study had 29 people. Studies lasted from 40 days to five years.

Anterior versus posterior approaches: there may be little to no difference between the two approaches in how well people can perform daily tasks, their functional status, mortality, or pain at three months after surgery, but we are very uncertain about the results. No studies looked at health-related quality of life within four months of surgery.

Anterior versus lateral approaches: there may be little to no difference between the two approaches in how well people can perform daily tasks, or in their functional status or pain at three months after surgery, but we are very uncertain about the results. We found the anterior approach may reduce the presence of a limp slightly at three months after surgery. No studies looked at health-related quality of life within four months of surgery. We are unsure of the effect on mortality within four months of surgery.

Lateral versus posterior approaches: there may be little to no difference between the two methods in how well people can perform daily tasks, or in their health-related quality of life, functional status or pain at three months after surgery, but we are very uncertain about the results. There may also be no difference between the methods in the risk of dying within three months of surgery.

## What are the limitations of the evidence?

In general, we have low or very low confidence in the current level of evidence. Two primary factors reduced our confidence in the evidence. First, there were not enough people in the studies to be certain about their findings, and the results were very inconsistent across the different studies. Second, small study sizes limited the ability to detect rare but clinically important unwanted effects, which were often not reported or were inadequately described.

## How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is up to date to 1 November 2024. Studies were published between 1981 and 2024.

# YYYInterventions

## General details

* **Surgeon:** Eight surgeons, with four in each intervention group, each with minimum 15 years experience.

* **Components:** Cemented Mueller Straight Stem (Zimmer, Muensingen, Switzerland)

* **anaesthesia:** Spinal or general, anaesthesia choice

* **Care protocol:** Standardised multimodal pain regimen, Full weightbearing, Physical therapist-led mobilisation post op day 2. Suture removal post op day 10. Discharge for rehabilitation post op day 10 to 14.

## Intervention group 1 (Anterior)

Anterior modified Smith-Peterson approach.

"The patient is positioned on the operating table in the supine position. Both legs are draped in a sterile fashion. A straight skin incision 10 cm to 12 cm in length is performed; the starting point is 1 cm distal to and 1 cm lateral to the anterior superior iliac spine, and the end point is at the same height in line with the upper aspect of the greater trochanter. The anterior rim of the tensor fascia lata muscle is identified, and the fascia is dissected in line with the skin incision. Using blunt dissection, crossing vessels are cauterised and dissected around the medial side of the tensor muscle. The rectus femoris muscle is then mobilised medially, whereas the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles are held laterally. This exposes the hip capsule that is subsequently excised. For improved access to the femur, the surgical limb is positioned in external rotation under the contralateral leg, and the operating table is lowered by ∼30-degree angle. Next, an osteotomy of the femoral neck is performed 1 cm proximal to the lesser trochanter, directed 45-degree angle in the anteroposterior direction. After the preparation of the femur, a Mueller Straight Stem is cemented in place, followed by attachment of a hemiprosthesis head. In cases of intraoperative instability, a bipolar head is implanted. The procedure is completed with a layered closure."

## Intervention group 2 (Lateral)

Hardinge direct lateral approach.

"The patient is placed in supine position, and the operative limb is flexibly draped in a sterile fashion. From the upper margin of the greater trochanter, a 10-cm to 12-cm a skin incision is made following the axis of the femur and ending at approximately the same height with the anterior superior iliac spine. The fascia lata is incised and split both proximally and distally. Trochanteric bursa tissue is excised, and the tendons of the gluteus medius and vastus lateralis muscles are exposed. At the junction between anterior and middle third of the greater trochanter, a musculoperioseteal sleeve is separated from the greater trochanter using electrocautery. Next, the ventral fibres of the gluteus medius and the vastus lateralis muscles are retracted together as a unit. This exposes the hip capsule that is subsequently excised. The osteotomy of the femoral neck is then performed 1 cm proximal to the lesser trochanter. After removal of the femoral head, the proximal femur is exposed and prepared. Next, a Mueller Straight Stem is cemented in place, and a hemiprosthesis head is attached. In cases of intraoperative instability, a bipolar head is implanted. The dissected part of the gluteus medius tendon is reinserted using a transosseous technique. The procedure is completed with a layered closure."

## General details

* **Surgeon:** Not reported

* **Components:** Cobalt chrome alloy stem, bipolar head, 41 press-fit, 2 cemented stem

* **Anaesthesia:** Not reported

* **Care protocol:** After admission, patients were actively treated for comorbidities, underwent preoperative preparation, and received preoperative education. Once the preoperative preparation was completed, the surgery was scheduled. Both procedures were performed with the patient in a standard lateral position. There were no specific positioning requirements for the SuperPATH group. However, for the anterolateral group, special restrictions were applied: "D-shaped shoe," internal rotation of the lower limbs, and abduction. When lying on the unaffected side, a pillow was placed between the legs to prevent adduction and external rotation of the lower limb. Both groups received prophylactic anticoagulant medication, using rivaroxaban, which continued as part of their ongoing treatment. After the anaesthesia wore off, active movement was encouraged. For the SuperPATH group, patients were encouraged to walk with the assistance of a walking aid or crutches on the second day after surgery, without any specific range of motion restrictions. For the anterolateral group, patients were allowed to walk on the ground after one week, with toes pointing forward. They were instructed to avoid hip flexion exceeding 90°, external rotation of the affected limb, and crossing their legs for six months. Regular follow-up examinations were scheduled at 3 and 6 months postoperatively, and then annually.

## Intervention group 1 (Posterior)

"Conventional Instrumentation SuperPATH Approach (Experimental Group) [5-7]: The hip joint was flexed to approximately 60°, internally rotated by 20°, and slightly adducted. Along the axis of the femur, a longitudinal incision was made starting approximately 2 cm below the tip of the greater trochanter, extending proximally for about 8 cm. The gluteus maximus muscle was bluntly separated and retracted to expose the gluteus medius muscle. Instead of using the specialised retractor for SuperPATH technique, a conventional "S" hook was used to retract the gluteus medius muscle anteriorly, revealing the piriformis muscle and the gluteus minimus muscle. At this point, unnamed vessels crossing the surgical field were often visible, and electrocoagulation was performed to control bleeding and avoid interference with the surgical process. Access was gained through the gap between the piriformis and gluteus minimus muscles, entering the joint capsule beneath. The capsule could be incised in a "T" or "L" shape, revealing the femoral neck and acetabulum, as well as the intertrochanteric fossa and the apex of the greater trochanter. Two commonly used acetabular hooks were used instead of the specialised blunt hook for SuperPATH, inserted along the anterior and posterior aspects of the femoral neck cortex, allowing simultaneous retraction of the joint capsule and surrounding muscle groups, resulting in good exposure of the surgical field. Under direct visualization, fracture reduction could usually be easily achieved, which helped determine the anteversion angle (or based on the residual axis of the fracture ends). A Kirschner wire could be used as a substitute for SuperPATH to determine the direction of the femoral medullary cavity."

## Intervention group 2 (Lateral)

"Conventional Instrumentation Anterolateral Approach (Control Group) [8]: A modified Hardinge approach was used, where the iliotibial tract was bluntly separated, and the gluteus medius muscle was retracted. The anterior one-third of the gluteus medius muscle and the gluteus minimus muscle were cut near their insertions, and the retracted muscles were then mobilized inward. This provided good exposure to the anterior aspect of the joint capsule, which was then excised. The femoral neck was preserved approximately 1.0 cm, and osteotomy was performed to remove the femoral head. The diameter was measured, and an appropriate femoral head was selected. The femoral side was opened, the medullary canal was reamed distally, and the proximal portion was shaped. After successful completion, the joint was irrigated, and the prosthesis was implanted. In the case of a cemented prosthesis, a medullary canal plug was placed, followed by insertion of an exhaust tube. After injecting bone cement, the exhaust tube was removed, and the femoral stem containing the intermediate component was inserted, ensuring no overflow. After solidification, neck length was checked, and the dual articulation head was installed. Finally, reduction was performed, and the joint was tested for movement in all directions without impingement, stable and not dislocating, with good tension. Extensive irrigation was performed, and approximately 50 mL of tranexamic acid solution was injected into the surrounding soft tissues to reduce bleeding. After confirming no active bleeding, the joint capsule was sutured and repaired, and the decision to place a drain was based on the presence of exudate. The incision was closed."

## Intervention group 1 (Lateral)

"Patient in supine position. Exposure is made through a longitudinal incision beginning about 5 cm proximal and continuing over the tip of the greater trochanter and extends down the line of the femur shaft for 8 cm. Incise fascia lata in line with the skin incision. Retract the fascia lata anteriorly and the gluteus maximus posteriorly. Blunt dissection of any fibers of gluteus medius that attach to fascia lata. Insertion of the gluteus medius through a crescent shaped course 3-5 cm above the greater trochanter and extend the incision inferior through the fibers of vastus lateralis. Develop an anterior flap by sharp dissection of anterior gluteus medius fibers and the anterior part of the vastus laterals of the bone. Exposure of the hip joint is reached by releasing the gluteus minimus from the antererior greater trochanter to expose and dissect the anterior joint capsule...The stronger posterior capsule is preserved. When closing the hip joint the capsule is sutured as well as the fibers of the vastus lateralis and gluteus medius."

## Intervention group 2 (Posterior)

"Patient in side position. Exposure is made through a 10-15 cm curved incision that begins about 7 cm cranial and posterior of the greater trochanter and continue across the greater trochanter down towards the femur shaft. In line with the skin incision, the fascia lata is incised to exposure the distal vastus lateralis. The gluteus maximus muscle is separated by blunt dissection. Stretch the short external rotators and detach the piriformis and obturator internus muscle. Expose the hip joint by a longitudinally incision of the posterior capsule. Dislocate the hip with internal rotation after capsulotomy...The gluteus medius and vastus lateralis are preserved. When closing the hip joint the capsule is sutured and the piriformis is reattached. plain_language_summary.S:
What are the benefits and risks of different ways of accessing the hip joint during partial hip replacement surgery?

## Key messages

* The evidence is still developing, and future studies may change our conclusions.
* We are not confident that one surgical approach (way of accessing the hip joint) compared to another leads to a different outcome for performing daily tasks, health-related quality of life, mobility or functional status, mortality, or pain, within the first four months after surgery.

## What is hip hemiarthroplasty?

Hip hemiarthroplasty, or partial hip replacement, is surgery that replaces the ball of the thighbone (femur) with an artificial one, leaving the socket untouched.

## Why is this important for people with hip fractures?

Hip fractures are common, especially in older adults. They can be very painful and make it hard to walk or live independently. Partial hip replacement is a way to fix these fractures, reducing pain, and getting people back on their feet faster. There are different ways to access the hip joint during surgery (approaches). Each has its own benefits and drawbacks.

## What did we want to find out?

We wanted to find out what effect different surgical approaches for performing a partial hip replacement can have on a person recovering from surgery.

## What did we do?

We searched for studies comparing different approaches for partial hip replacement. Studies had to choose people at random (or use their dates of birth or alternate methods) for each approach and then follow their recovery after surgery. Studies included adults with hip fractures. We compared and summarised the study results, and rated our confidence in the evidence, based on factors such as study size and methods.

## What did we find?

We found 27 studies with 3369 people. Studies took place throughout Europe and Asia. The biggest study had 843 people and the smallest study had 29 people. Studies lasted from 40 days to five years.

Anterior versus posterior approaches: there may be little to no difference between the two approaches in how well people can perform daily tasks, their functional status, mortality, or pain at three months after surgery, but we are very uncertain about the results. No studies looked at health-related quality of life within four months of surgery.

Anterior versus lateral approaches: there may be little to no difference between the two approaches in how well people can perform daily tasks, or in their functional status or pain at three months after surgery, but we are very uncertain about the results. We found the anterior approach may reduce the presence of a limp slightly at three months after surgery. No studies looked at health-related quality of life within four months of surgery. We are unsure of the effect on mortality within four months of surgery.

Lateral versus posterior approaches: there may be little to no difference between the two methods in how well people can perform daily tasks, or in their health-related quality of life, functional status or pain at three months after surgery, but we are very uncertain about the results. There may also be no difference between the methods in the risk of dying within three months of surgery.

## What are the limitations of the evidence?

In general, we have low or very low confidence in the current level of evidence. Two primary factors reduced our confidence in the evidence. First, there were not enough people in the studies to be certain about their findings, and the results were very inconsistent across the different studies. Second, small study sizes limited the ability to detect rare but clinically important unwanted effects, which were often not reported or were inadequately described.

## How up to date is this evidence?

The evidence is up to date to 1 November 2024. Studies were published between 1981 and 2024.

YYYPlain language summary:

## Are virtual reality interventions more effective than an alternative or no intervention for the rehabilitation of people with multiple sclerosis?

### Key messages

* Virtual reality might improve balance and postural control, upper limb function, and participation and quality of life, but the overall quality of the evidence is limited.
* Since these results are based on few studies of lower quality, they should be interpreted with caution.

### What is multiple sclerosis?

Multiple sclerosis is the most common neurological disease in young adults. People with multiple sclerosis can have a variety of symptoms, such as fatigue, and sensory, cognitive and sexual dysfunction, but also muscle weakness and co-ordination problems.

### How can virtual reality help people with multiple sclerosis?

Virtual reality has been proposed as a new rehabilitation tool and is increasingly being used for the rehabilitation of neurological patients. Virtual reality interventions use computer programs that allow users to navigate in and interact with a virtual environment. The use of virtual reality in rehabilitation offers several advantages, such as providing fully controllable, personalised environments and situations that are too dangerous, expensive or impossible in real life. Moreover, the level of difficulty and intensity can be adapted to the skills of the patient, and virtual reality has the potential to increase patients’ motivation by creating more exciting training environments and providing feedback.

### What did we want to find out?

The purpose of this review was to assess the effectiveness of virtual reality interventions for the rehabilitation of people with multiple sclerosis. We wanted to find out whether training with virtual reality resulted in more improvement of lower limb function and gait, balance and postural control, upper limb function, cognition, fatigue, global motor function, activity limitations, participation and quality of life, and the occurrence of adverse (harmful or unwanted) events. We compared virtual reality training to 1) no intervention and 2) conventional therapy or an alternative therapy.

### What did we do?

We identified 33 studies with a total of 1294 people with multiple sclerosis, who on average (based on 22 studies) had a significant disability but were able to walk without an aid for 500 metres. A lot of different virtual reality devices and programs were used. Almost 91% (30) of the included studies used non-immersive virtual reality systems (e.g. TV screens), two studies used semi-immersive virtual reality devices (e.g. big screens) and one study used a full-immersive head-mounted display. Most virtual reality interventions aimed to improve balance and gait function.

### What did we find?

Ten studies assessed whether virtual reality can be used to improve gait and balance function and found that the use of virtual reality may not result in better function for most outcome measures when compared to no intervention (we are very uncertain about these results). When compared to conventional therapy, the gains in terms of lower limb and gait function were probably not greater for the virtual reality interventions. However, virtual reality is probably superior in improving balance and postural control compared to conventional therapy.

Two trials tested whether virtual reality would lead to more improvements in upper limb function compared to no intervention, and found that this may be the case. Virtual reality may be more effective in improving upper limb function than conventional therapy. Studies that assessed participation and quality of life may indicate positive effects in favour of virtual reality, both when compared to no intervention and conventional therapy (we are very uncertain about these results). We were unable to assess the effect of virtual reality interventions on global motor function and adverse events.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

Overall, we have moderate to low or very low confidence in evidence. This was mainly due to the small numbers of participants in the included studies and the poor quality of the studies. Moreover, due to the nature of the included studies, the evidence is mainly limited to people with a relatively low degree of physical disability and virtual reality technology that has a limited degree of immersion. Furthermore, the methods used in the studies varied; for example, regarding the types of outcomes measured and the design of the interventions.

### How up-to-date is this evidence?

The evidence is current to August 2022.

## Are virtual reality interventions more effective than an alternative or no intervention for the rehabilitation of people with multiple sclerosis?

### Key messages

* Virtual reality might improve balance and postural control, upper limb function, and participation and quality of life, but the overall quality of the evidence is limited.
* Since these results are based on few studies of lower quality, they should be interpreted with caution.

### What is multiple sclerosis?

Multiple sclerosis is the most common neurological disease in young adults. People with multiple sclerosis can have a variety of symptoms, such as fatigue, and sensory, cognitive and sexual dysfunction, but also muscle weakness and co-ordination problems.

### How can virtual reality help people with multiple sclerosis?

Virtual reality has been proposed as a new rehabilitation tool and is increasingly being used for the rehabilitation of neurological patients. Virtual reality interventions use computer programs that allow users to navigate in and interact with a virtual environment. The use of virtual reality in rehabilitation offers several advantages, such as providing fully controllable, personalised environments and situations that are too dangerous, expensive or impossible in real life. Moreover, the level of difficulty and intensity can be adapted to the skills of the patient, and virtual reality has the potential to increase patients’ motivation by creating more exciting training environments and providing feedback.

### What did we want to find out?

The purpose of this review was to assess the effectiveness of virtual reality interventions for the rehabilitation of people with multiple sclerosis. We wanted to find out whether training with virtual reality resulted in more improvement of lower limb function and gait, balance and postural control, upper limb function, cognition, fatigue, global motor function, activity limitations, participation and quality of life, and the occurrence of adverse (harmful or unwanted) events. We compared virtual reality training to 1) no intervention and 2) conventional therapy or an alternative therapy.

### What did we do?

We identified 33 studies with a total of 1294 people with multiple sclerosis, who on average (based on 22 studies) had a significant disability but were able to walk without an aid for 500 metres. A lot of different virtual reality devices and programs were used. Almost 91% (30) of the included studies used non-immersive virtual reality systems (e.g. TV screens), two studies used semi-immersive virtual reality devices (e.g. big screens) and one study used a full-immersive head-mounted display. Most virtual reality interventions aimed to improve balance and gait function.

### What did we find?

Ten studies assessed whether virtual reality can be used to improve gait and balance function and found that the use of virtual reality may not result in better function for most outcome measures when compared to no intervention (we are very uncertain about these results). When compared to conventional therapy, the gains in terms of lower limb and gait function were probably not greater for the virtual reality interventions. However, virtual reality is probably superior in improving balance and postural control compared to conventional therapy.

Two trials tested whether virtual reality would lead to more improvements in upper limb function compared to no intervention, and found that this may be the case. Virtual reality may be more effective in improving upper limb function than conventional therapy. Studies that assessed participation and quality of life may indicate positive effects in favour of virtual reality, both when compared to no intervention and conventional therapy (we are very uncertain about these results). We were unable to assess the effect of virtual reality interventions on global motor function and adverse events.

### What are the limitations of the evidence?

Overall, we have moderate to low or very low confidence in evidence. This was mainly due to the small numbers of participants in the included studies and the poor quality of the studies. Moreover, due to the nature of the included studies, the evidence is mainly limited to people with a relatively low degree of physical disability and virtual reality technology that has a limited degree of immersion. Furthermore, the methods used in the studies varied; for example, regarding the types of outcomes measured and the design of the interventions.

### How up-to-date is this evidence?

The evidence is current to August 2022.
